Although Judge Charbonneau's judgment clears the air, it does not settle the question. It is not the judgment of a final tribunal, and there are other decisions which conflict with it. Even if a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada or the Judicial Committee be obtained it may not cover the whole ground.
The Dominion parliament ought to enact a law covering the full extent of its power. At present, although it is generally admitted that the Dominion Parliament has full power to declare who shall and who shall not be competent to marry, the federal statute legalizes a marriage with a deceased wife's sister. The law should set forth exactly what are the prohibitions to marriage. It should declare that no spiritual court has any power to annul a marriage or grant a divorce, and impose a penalty upon any person attempting to exercise that authority.
Mr. Holmested, in his book on the marriage law, says that all provincial courts which now grant divorce should be superseded by a Dominion court. At present the law is not uniform, and the administration is not uniform. In the maritime provinces and in British Columbia there are divorce courts; and there is a different law on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. In the other provinces there is no divorce court, and resort must be made to the Senate. It is easy to see how this diversity would facilitate the making of unfounded claims to authority in the province of Quebec.
A Dominion statute, covering the grounds thoroughly, would be a strong assertion of the civil power, which would tend to discourage usurpations and unfounded claims to authority. It is true that the provinces have power to deal with solemnization. But the question of solemnization may be confused with that of competence. Thus, in Quebec, the attempt was made to distinguish between the kind of solemnization necessary for Protestants and the kind necessary for Catholics.
It may also be found that provincial legislation is necessary. Mr. Holmested, for instance, says that a minister should be forbidden to exact, as a condition of solemnizing marriage, any condition as to the education of children. It mav be necessary also to make further provisions for surrounding the solemnization of marriage with safeguards, and protecting innocent parties from deception. The more strongly and definitely the civil power asserts itself, the less danger will there be of clerical interference. The State has been neglecting its duty; the remedy lies in its doing its duty.

What I asked my hon. friend is, whether he intends to have a general rule, applicable to all highways or whether each case shall be left to itself. There is a great deal in what the right hon. gentleman says, but I think that for the first few years at least the money should first be expended on the improvement of highways leaving the other matter to the counties in the province until later on at all events. Before the clause passes I have a word or two to say in reference to the matter. It seems that on the second reading of this Bill the general principle of road aid was pretty well admitted, and for very apparent reasons. The roads form an important part of the large problem of transportation, to which the government has given great attention. We can understand that the broad question of aid to roads would be a principle to be generally admitted. Transportation is one of the principle factors in the nationalization of our country. It is an important factor in commerce and in production, for without good roads the development of our country would be absolutely impossible. Of what avail would be the great crops of our farm and the products of our mines if there was not proper transportation to carry these products to the markets of the world? The good roads question has received the attention of the several provinces. Within comparatively recent years the province of Quebec took the matter up, and has now a measure before it to deal with the matter. Last year the province of Quebec spent about $400,000 on the development of highways. Previously its policy took the form of aiding the different parishes and the different municipalities, by making to them certain grants and paying for a certain proportion of the work. That scheme went on for several years and some advantage has been derived from it. Now it seems they are departing from that mode of giving aid, and have set aside $10,000,000 by which they propose to pay interest and a sinking fund to aid municipalities. That is to say the municipalities will borrow money for the purpose of the construction of roads, and the provincial government will undertake to
pay two per cent on the interest and two per cent on the sinking fund so that the debt will be eventually wiped off.
The amount of aid granted under this new system will not be materially more than the aid under the old system. Under the_ old system about $400,000 was granted, which is just the interest at 4 per cent on $10,000,000. But, for some reason or other the Quebec government felt that they would rather have the money in their pocket in order to deal with the matter in this new way. I would not presume to venture an opinion, but perhaps they feel that the way to their return to power in the next provincial elections would be improved, if they had the money in their pockets
Is that the way you feel about this measure so far as the federal government is concerned?

I have no particularly keen feeling about the measure, Mr. Chairman; I am only remarking that though the scheme in relation to Quebec is changed, yet the amount of aid is not really materially increased; and some of us are of the opinion that the fact that the general elections are about to come off in Quebec may have something to do with the change of system, and the desire of the government to have cash in their pockets before they discuss the question of highways. That may or may not be, but from experience in the past, some of us hold that opinion. Now, in Quebec the dealing is directly with the municipality; each parish, each township is dealt with directly by the government in constructing these good roads. In Ontario, the system is different. Before the Ontario government will aid in the development of roads, the county must take over the roads, lay out a large county system and then expend the money in the development of that system. In that way in Ontario they would have between forty and fifty county systems, which, you can readily understand, could be developed into a provincial system. But in the province of Quebec, dealing as they do with municipalities, parishes and .townships, they would have about six hundred separate systems, about six hundred different modes of building roads, making it much more difficult to reconcile differences and unite all in a provincial system. Viewing this question from a Dominion point of view, my opinion is that we must not come in too close contact with the separate municipalities. We must keep at a view point from which we can see the system as a whole and consider its advantages to the Dominion as a whole. Therefore, it seems to me better to deal with the provinces than with the municipalities. Although I am interested in getting all possible aid for for the province of Quebec, yet I am in



regard to the topography of the country. In many cases it will 'be found expedient to build around grades and hills which will make the road very much easier and, therefore, much more useful to one public. Under the direction of a scientifically trained engineer, who understands the technical requirements of road planning and construction and who is familiar with the topography of the country, .a road could be built in such a way that its usefulness to the public would be very materially increased. By forming these roads in the provinces, by joining them up into Dominion roads, by having a Dominion highway when the time comes for it, and I trust it will not be very many years, an extra bond will be created to bind the different parts of this country together. The present bond of the railways has worked wonders, but the great distances between the stops, travelled at a high rate of speed, lessens the advantages of this mode of intercommunication as compared with the advantages that will be derived from a national highway. There will be upon the national highway greater intercourse between the people of the different provinces, there will be slower locomotion and the life on the roads will tend to bring the citizens of the different provinces shoulder to shoulder in daily intercourse, and will do much in the way of enabling the citizens of the different provinces to understand each other's weaknesses, and each other's strength. In that way there will grow up. I believe, through the aid granted to these national highways, one great Dominion fellowship the effect of which will be greatly enhanced by the existence and influence of such a gigantic work as that which is contemplated by the measure now before the committee. For these reasons I have great pleasure in supporting the Bill.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-the minister may undertake construction and improvement of highways,

I think the government is making a mistake in going into the construction of roads and not giving the money to the provinces. The provinces have now a system of road construction. Ontario went into the construction of roads some years ago. The government of Sir George Boss provided $1,000,000 to help the counties in building roads. About) twenty counties received the provincial aid. What the people want is not trunk roads. The Ontario Good Boads Association met the other day in Toronto and that opinion was expressed by many of its members, amongst whom was the president, who said that the people wanted township and Mr. BAKER.
county roads, and not trunk roads. The province, I think, is in a better position to build township and county roads than trunk roads. If the government is going to undertake to build roads it is going to duplicate the work of the provinces, and, therefore, it is going to spend tne money uselessly. I think the proposition of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), was right that the money should be given to the provinces according to population. The province of Quebec also inaugurated a system of good roads a few years ago, and it is going into the work this year very extensively. I believe that the people would get much more benefit from the money spent in this way 'than if the work were left to the Dominion. We want roads leading to the villages and towns, especially the county towns, to the local markets of the farmers, since we cannot get the American market. I therefore, propose that section 6 be stricken out.

Before this clause is considered I would like to say a word or two in order that I may understand really just what is the position of the government, in regard to this whole Bill. On the first reading of the Bill my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked the Minister of Bailways, the following question:
I would ask the hon. gentleman to tell us if there is any basis of allotment among the provinces. The provincial subsidies are based on population; is this based on population?
The Minister of Bailways and Canals said:
It is to be on the same basis as that on which subsidies are granted to the provinces, in other words, by population.
What page? ,

That is read by the minister at page 3734 of ' Hansard.' When this Bill was introduced and discussed on the second reading it clearly went on the assumption that we were dealing with a proposition by the government to grant to each one of the provinces, under a system which would be on a parity with that which exists in regard to subsidies, a certain sum of money to be devoted to tire improvement of roads.
Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Bill contemplate the federal government making a grant to the provincial government in aid of the construction of roads, the presumption being that the expenditure would be made by the provincial government. I do not think there can be any objection to that method, but if that method be not pursued, then we will have a most curious jumbled up system of road expenditure in the country. Apparently, under the first five sections of the Bill, the idea is, that the Dominion gov-

eriiment will, in agreement with the provincial government, utilize all the provincial and municipal machinery and have a unification of authority and a practical working out of a system under which the roads will get the benefit of the money without _ any unnecessary expenditure for supervision or inspection by the federal government. But section 6 is entirely out of touch with that theory. Under section 6 it apparently is contemplated to originate a new system of expenditure by the federal government in the construction of roads, entirely apart from the provincial and municipal arrangements. The Prime Minister argued the other day that at the end of section 6, there was a limitation, because the federal government had to obtain the authority of the provincial legislature and the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, but that addendum does not mean anything at all, because it was not possible for the federal government to enact any law that would enable it to spend any money upon any provincial road in this country without the consent of the provincial government or the municipality that owned the roads. The officers of the federal government would be trespassers if they ventured to go on any road anywhere in Canada without the consent of the provincial government. The important feature of this is that under section 6, the minister is given power to take the whole amount allotted to any province to expend it as he pleases. We ought to be frankly told what the policy of the government on this question is, because if it be as I have indicated then I would move that the clause be stricken out. I submit that the provinces are the proper authorities to deal with the roads; they own them, they have for fifty years provided machinery for making and approving them.
Did you not say that the townships owned the roads?
Yes.
Thena according to your view, we would have to go back to the townships.

Certainly, you would have to go to the municipalities. If the minister expends any money on roads in Nova Scotia he would have to go to the municipalities. Not only that, but we have the statute labour system there under which every person who lives along the highway is compelled to contribute in labour or money annually for its maintenance. The provinces have had years of experience of working in conjunction with the municipalities; they have provincial engineers who know all about the character of the soil and the difficulties to be met with in permanent road construction and drain-mi
age, all of which must be considered when you come to expend money on roads, and if the federal government is to spend the money, exercising only its own judgment, then we will be throwing away the experience of fifty years that the provinces and the municipalities have had in road construction. Where you have had wise expenditure on roads by municipalities and provinces, and in view of the growing public opinion and the growing interest in favour of good roads, it seems to me that the federal government should not directly enter into the arena and complicate the whole situation. I can conceive that the federal government could render valuable aid in this matter by the establishment of a good roads bureau such as the federal government has established in the United States, and by which uniformity of conditions could be brought about throughout the Dominion. But, if the federal government is going to undertake the work of constructing roads themselves, I believe they will throw away a tremendous lot of money on inspection and supervision before they get down to actual real expenditure of money on the roads themselves. The first five clauses of the Bill, with certain amendments which have been suggested, would meet with my approval, but section 6 is entirely in subversion of the principles laid down in the previous clauses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It seems to me that my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) is unduly disturbed about this. The first part of the Bill provides for grants out of the federal treasury to the provinces, under certain safeguards as to expenditure, cost of construction and various other considerations which ought he taken into account, and my hon. friend is willing that these sections should become law, while to section 6 he strongly objects. Well, the sixth section provides that where the government of a province is willing, the federal government may undertake the work itself instead of handing the money over to the province, and that seems to be a very proper provision. The hon. member inquires whether there is to be a general policy of federal expenditure under this section in every province of Canada.
No one could give him that information in the first instance, 'because I am sure he would be the first to understand that the efficiency of the organization may vary greatly in different provinces. In one province you may have a thoroughly effective system, under which the construction and improvement and maintenance of highways are carried on. In such a province it is perfectly clear that the best course would be to hand the money over to the provincial government or under some ar-

rangement with the provincial government, so that the existing official organization anight be made use of in the expenditure of money. But it may happen that in some other province the organization is not very effective, and that the provincial government itself, under the authority of the provincial legislature, might desire the expenditure of the proposed aid in this way. If such a condition should arise, the money could only be expended in that way with the consent of the province. I see no reason why authority should not be given in this Bill to enable a proposal of that kind to be carried out. It was for that reason that this clause was inserted in the Bill. It is possible that it may be used only very occasionally, but, whether occasionally or otherwise, it seems to me to be one to which no valid objection can be made, and one which might be found very useful in carrying out the proposal of the government for the improvement of highways in the various provinces.
What organization does the right hon. gentleman refer to when he says that the organization in some of the provinces may be effective?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The organization of the road service.

I want to ask the Prime Minister a question in reference to this matter. This is one of the most important proposals ever made in the country, and the government deserve great credit for it. What I want to see is something that- can be worked out in a practical way to bring the greatest good to the farmers who use ilihe Ihighways. The federal government might make a grant of a certain percentage, to be supplemented by the provincial government wherever the people in any community agree to raise a certain amount for the purpose, and then have the counties take over and maintain these roadways thereafter at their own expense. The community in which I am interested is ready at the present time to raise a certain amount of money; but how can it under this Act get the assistance it wants from the provincial and federal governments, and then get the money expended in a way that will secure permanent roadways by having uniform specifications and a method of construction that will ensure the judicious expending of the money? If the community wishes to get the assistance that is supposed to be within its reach through the medium of this Bill, how can that be worked out so that the parties will all come together and build these roadways?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can say to my hon. friend, who has made a very practical suggestion, that in the course of preparing this Bill a good many suggestions more or less Mr. BORDEN
along the line which he has mentioned were brought to our attention. We had under consideration the placing in this Bill of some percentage which must be provided by the province and by the municipality if a certain other percentage were provided by the federal government; but it was impossible to get the necessary information as to conditions in all the provinces of Canada to justify us in fixing a hard and fast rule of that kind in this Bill. I would like to assure my hon. friend that the idea which he has just presented very clearly to the House is one that has been in the mind of the government, and I would like also to assure him that it would be perfectly possible under the provisions of this Bill to work out a scheme of that kind, and it is for that reason that the provisions of this Bill are couched in the general form in which they now appear.

The question at present 'before the House is not one connected with the general purpose of the Bill. That general purpose is to aid out of the federal treasury in the building of highways. Up to the present time this has been considered to be not only a provincial work but a municipal work. Section 6 is not at all a corollary of the previous sections. All the previous sections converge to one idea, that is, that the money should be voted by parliament and should be expended by the provinces or in concert with the provinces. But the section now under consideration defeats to a large extent the previous sections. It provides that the money, instead of being handed over to the provinces to be by them expended, may be expended by the Dominion government or by the Minister of Railways. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has I think very properly suggested the objection there is to investing the Minister of Railways with such a power as is described in that section, and the only answer which the Prime Minister has made is that if it is to be done at all, it must be done by the Governor in Council. So far so good. What I say is that there should not be even the power to make such a bargain with the local governments. This work is not intended and cannot be intended to come within the purview of the federal parliament. It cannot be contended that it was ever the intention of the British North America Act, in making a division of powers between the local legislatures and the Dominion parliament, that the Dominion government should become highway constructors. The fathers of Confederation laid dowrn very clearly what should be the duties of the local legislatures and what should be the duties of the Dominion parliament. We are going to some extent out of our way, but sti' 1 we are within our

jurisdiction, when we provide that out of the federal treasury assistance shall be given to the provinces, not for general purposes, but for one specific object, that is to say, the making or improving of highways.
But, Sir, it is conceivable if the Railway Department is going to become a constructor of highways that it will be able to do the work to-iday which is done by the local legislature? It is part, and a most important part, of the duties of the local legislatures to look after highways, and as has been stated by my hon. friend from Piotou (Mar. Macdonald), a moment ago, they have a special organization for that purpose. 'That money should be supplied to them, more than they have been given, for the purpose of making or improving highways, is accepted by 'everybody, but, Sir, power is given now to the Minister of Raiways to inaugurate a new system altogether, and himself to become the contractor or builder of these roads. That in my humble judgment, as reducing very much the usefulness of the Minister of Railways. At present the minister has only to do with administering the railways and canals of the country. If, in addition, to that, he is given the subsidiary task of looking .after the highways of the country be must have a new staff, a new organization. What reason can there be why the organization which now exists in all the provinces should not be continued as it is at the present time? The policy proposed can be carried out with the consent of the provinces I know, but I repeat that it is not at all in accordance with the spirit of the constitution, and I can conceive of no reason why there will be more advantage in having this work performed by the Minister of Railways than by any of the provincial governments. The minister is not equipped for this work, it has never 'been the object of his department to do it, it is a new thing altogether, and when the machinery already exists in the provinces to carry out the work which is intended, I cannot see why new machinery should ,be organized, which, in the nature of things, cannot construct highways as efficiently as that construction must and can be done by the local authorities.
'Mr. DEVLIN. Unfortunately when the first discussion in connection with this measure took place I was not in my seat. Like a good many hon. gentlemen oppoisite I was engaged in examining the highways-

And the byways.
Mr. DEVLIN-and the byways of the county of 'South Renfrew, and so I must apoligize if some of the remarks I may make this afternoon might have been
delivered at an earlier stage. I want to say that I am entirely in favour of aniy aid which may be given to the highways of our country, but I think there should be some provision in the Bill by which the money grant to toe made under it shall reach the municipalities and the portions of a county where the money is most needed. I asked the Prime Minister a moment ago what nature of 'organization he was referring to when he said that the money would be given either to the organization or to the Minister of Railways, to act in conjuction with the organization in this province. From my modest experience in matters of organization when dealing with the government of the day, the only organizations I know of are political organizations, and I hardly think that it would 'be in the interest of the country, much less in the interest of the rural municipalities, that the Minister oif Railways should toe let loose to deal with political organizations in handling the money of the country given for the purpose of aiding in the construction of roads. I would very modestly suggest to the government that they go about this matter of improving our highways in a more systematic manner. Speaking more particularly for the province of Quebec, I know of no particular organization *such as that to which the Finance Minister refers. The custom there is for the legislature to vote a certain amount which is placed at the disposal of the Minister of Colonization. That minister visits the different parts of the province and studies the local needs personally and accepts advice from those who are most concerned in the matter of municipal roads, how best to expend the provincial funds in improving colonization and other roads. There is absolutely no such provision in this Bill. In the province of Quebec the money is handed over to some party who is directly interested-and preferably to the municipalities-somebody who is authorized by the municipalities to expend that money. If the government of the day were to establish a system by which they would hand first to the provinces a set sum of money with the understanding that the provinces would get into touch with the counties, and that that money should be expended for the purpose first of municipal roads, then county roads, and then provincial and interprovincial roads, all parts of the country would be benefited. But to say that the Minister of Railways shall go forth with a sum of money in his pockets and meet his friends in the different counties and have the right to expend that money is simply ridiculous. That money will not reach the portions of the country where it is most needed for the highways. On the other hand, if by this Bill the gov-

emment of the day, through the Minister of Railways, is forced to expend that money right in the municipalities where it is needed, then I conceive that this Bill will work for the greater advantage of the country. I believe that no amount of money, properly expended, will be too great to aid in the construction of roads in this country; but I want to see the money reach the proper source, and under the Bill in its present form I cannot possibly see how that will occur. I know that the Minister of Railways, having power to expend this money right and left, will want to disburse it for the greater advantage of the country, but if he goes into the county of Wright, for instance, I hardly think he will go to any of those who may be friends of this political party and ask their advice. Rather will he go to the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite, and spend that money in those portions of the county which will benefit the party to whom that expenditure has been entrusted. I say without taking a partisan view at all of the subject-
Hear, hear.

I am in earnest in that statement because I foresee that the moment this Bill becomes law it will be placed in operation by the present government. But in a few years' time, perhaps sooner, hon. gentlemen may have changed places, and we on this side of the House may take their seats and operate the Bill to the disadvantage of municipalities that may not be exactly in sympathy with the political views wthich they entertain. Now is the time, whilst the Bill is under consideration, to insert provisions which will prevent any operation of the measure against the advantage of the whole country, so that neither hon. gentlemen opposite, nor any other political party for the time being in power, will be able to use the people's money for any other purpose, good, bad or indifferent, than the improvement of the highways and the byways of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I think this clause, giving the minister power to go throughout the country with the people's money in his pocket, and to expend it where he will, without any rider attached to the clause, is a very dangerous power to give to any gentleman in this House or in the government. I do not wish to hamper the government in any way in improving the highways of this country, but I would like to see the people's money reach a proper object.

Living close to the province of Ontario as the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) does, and having taken, as he has always taken, a lively interest tm Ontario provincial politics, he has probably heard from hon. members on his own side, who have been in the local Mr. DEVLIN.
legislature, how their friends, when in power in Ontario, annually dispensed an amount of approximately half a million dollars on roads in that province. And he probably knows that his political friends got good political results from the plan which he says might be followed by this government in the expenditure of the moneys under this proposed new system.. But I hope for the sake of the government, and for the reputation of the Dominion, that this government will not resort to the means resorted to by the hon. gentleman's friends in Ontario in road expenditure.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question? Under the clause as it stands, if the political party in power in this country, wishes to do so, will they not be able to carry out the plan which he condemns?

I think my hon. friend is unduly afraid that the bad example set by his friends in Ontario-and it may be also in the province of Quebec- will be followed. And, knowing that this plan was used very successfully from a political point of view by his friends in Ontario, he thinks the same force may be arrayed against him under the present proposal. But the principle here is a larger one. It contemplates probably a very large expenditure. And as this whole plan rises above the realm of party politics, I think the people of the Dominion will feel secure in the belief that this fund will be administered rightly, and not merely for political purposes, as was unfortunately the case in the province of Ontario for so many years. Speaking for myself, and I think I voice the sentiments of hon. gentlemen on this side, I would be loath to believe that a Minister of Railways and Canlals, representing the government of the day, would ever resort to mere pettifogging in the matter of this expenditure. I believe the whole scheme will be a broad, comprehensive one that will enure not only to, the political advantage of the party now in power, but to the practical advantage of each province where the work may be undertaken.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) answer me a question? 1s there not every year in the estimates a very large aggregate amount voted for dredging? And is not the Minister of Public Works empowered to spend that grant as he will? I have not charged my memory with the amount of this vote for each province, but it is a very large sum, and it is not voted for any particular work.
Mr. DEVLIN But tenders must be *called for.

Not necessarily in every case. But the point is that the work is undertaken at the discretion of the minister. The expenditure of the money may be safeguarded afterwards by calling for tenders which is right; but the Minister of Public Works can allot the money to this work or that, as he *chooses, without asking the authority of parliament for that distribution of the vote.

If I may be allowed- and I do not wish to speak too often- that is a purely administrative matter. But here is a case where one gentleman will have the right to go about this broad Dominion expending money right and left wherever he likes without parliament being able to say a solitary word about it, and not always, perhaps, applying the money to an object to which this House would wish to have it applied.
But is it not exactly the case of the Minister of Public Works under the general grant for dredging?

I desire to say only a few words in support of the arguments of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on the constitutional aspect of this clause. We havei heard a great deal about the conservation of our wealth, the conservation of our resources and the conservation of our flag. I am in favour of conservation, and especially of the conservation of the flag. But, as a Canadian, I am in favour of the conservation of our constitution which is the best protection that our flag can have. A few years ago, the government of the day, increased the allowance made to the several provinces. This was done upon a plan which received the unanimous assent of the provinces themselves. For my part, I stated at the time my regret that the increase of subsidies to the provinces was not made larger, as I believed that the time would come when the provinces would have to come back to the Dominion government for still further additions to their subsidies in order to efficiently maintain the schools and roads for which especially these subsidies are granted. I agree that it is an advantage to have more money spent upon our highways with a view to improving this means of communication throughout the Dominion. But I believe, as the right hon. leader of the opposition has said, that we should give the money to the provinces according to their population, the basis adopted years ago, and allow the provinces to distribute that money. This plan would avoid the friction which is certain otherwise to arise. It was stated in this debate a few days ago, I believe by an hon. gentleman on this side representing a Nova Scotia constituency, that, as the government of the province of Nova Scotia is a liberal government, it was likely to be discriminated against in the distribution of this money. I come from a province where the provincial government is to-day Conservative. But, as every member on the other side of the House knows, I am rather indifferent to the influence of any provincial government in any own riding, regardless of the money that may be at their disposal.
I say that according to the constitution, when you give money for local and provincial purposes, you should give it to be distributed by the provincial legislatures themselves, who are the properly constituted authorities for that purpose. That is the only way in which we can avoid future friction between the Dominion and the provincial governments. I have no doubt that the present Minister of Railways will endeavour to do the best he can. I am in favour of the federal government assisting the provinces to build roads; but my objection to this clause is based altogether on the constitutional ground that the money should be spent oy the provinces and not by the Dominion government, and that is why I shall oppose this clause.

I think the Minister of Railways would do well to take the advice tendered him this afternoon by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Baker). Of course, the member for Brome was not discussing section 6, he was discussing the general principle on which this money is to be spent. It is all very well for the member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) to defend the Minister of Railways, and say that he

will not do what the local government in Ontario did prior to 1905. I want to tell my hon. friend from East Simcoe that the old government of Ontario were human, the present government of Ontario is human, and so is the present Minister of Railways, and so will all the gentlemen be who will compose the Dominion government in all time to come. Now it may be that the Liberal government in Ontario were able to do everything crooked and wrong and that the present government may be able to do everything right. But I want to say that there is a Conservative government in power down in New Brunswick to-day who can do everything which the old Liberal government did in the province of Ontario; and I think I can ask this House to believe that it is possible that the present Minister of Railways may be influenced by his friends, at least in the province of New Brunswick, to do the very things that the member for East Simcoe objected to. Why, Sir, there is no use in mincing matters; the most, of us have had a hand in provincial politics, I have for one, the Minister of Railways has for another, and we all know how this road money has been bandied about and used as a matter of barter and sale from time immemorial. What I fear is that notwithstanding the good intentions of the Minister of Railways and the government as a whole, notwithstanding all their professions, the actual result will be, if this clause 6 becomes law, that they will be doing the very things which have been pointed out by the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) and others on this side of the House. If you want to know what the result will be, you have only to go back to South Renfrew during the last three weeks. There you find half-a-dozen government members of this House going the length and breadth of that riding, and telling the people: You should vote for the Conservative candidate because we are suing to give you a great slice out of this road money.

What did the minister say?
Mr. CARVELI,. I am only speaking of the men who are behind the minister. This will be the result if you place the Minister of Railways and Canals in a position of an ordinary road builder, and the pressure behind him will be so great that, I do not care who he may be, he will not be able to resist it. Even if this Bill provided that he should build permanent roads, it would not be so bad; if he had even said that he was going to drain his roads, it would not be so bad; it would have been much better if he had said: we must build a macadamized road with steel bridges and culverts.

But without one specification anywhere, without saying whether it is to be a permanent road or a mud road, every time an election is brought on, even a municipal election, you will find the changes will be rung, the party whip will be cracked and men will be told: ' If you don't vote for the county council we want you to vote for, you won't get any portion of this grant.' The member for Simcoe says: But we are bigger and broader than all that, this is a great national enterprise, we are going to run it on big broad lines. That is what we were told in New Brunswick before the elections of 1908; we were told that when the Conservative party got into power they were going to take the roads out of politics and hand them over entirely to the municipalities. They appointed in each parish a road board, composed of two municipal councillors, and a third man appointed by the government, and let me show you how it works out after three years of experience. In that province, we do not have local councils as they do in Ontario, we have municipal councils, consisting of two members from each parish, and all meet together in a county council. Wherever we have a Liberal and a Conservative on the road board, the government appoints a Conservative as a third man, and naturally he is the whole thing, he is president, secretary, treasurer, and the board is run on Conservative lines. Where we have two Liberal councillors, then invariably they are wholly ignored, and the road money is handled entirely by the man appointed by the government. I can tell him that there are dozens and dozens of road boards in the province of New Brunswick, that only meet once a year when they have to have an annual meeting, and they have squandered the money just as bad as it was squandered by these men that the member for East Simcoe was telling us about. Now they will be able to do these things in the future, just the same as they have done in the past, they will make these roads grants for purely political purposes. They j*will rake up the mud which was raked up the year before, and put it on top of the road, and they will pay the good money of the country for doing so, if they can get votes out of it. That is what they are doing in New Brunswick, and what they will continue to do under this Bill. _ Therefore, I think my hon. friends opposite must realize that this legislation is not in the spirit of the British North America Act. Does anybody suppose that when the British North America Act was framed a nroviso was put in making the Minister of Railways a road builder with a right to go on any highway and by way in any province and build roads?
This Bill does not give the minister that right.

Of course it does not say-so, there is a saving clause which says that permission must be obtained from the legislature. But does the Minister of Railways suppose that any legislature in Canada will refuse to allow him to go into that province and spend money on its roads? He knows better than that, he is not sincere in making that statement. Under the wording of this Bill he can give a $5 grant to build a little culvert if he thinks he can get a vote out of it; he can spend money on any road wholly or in part, and do absolutely as he likes with it. He does not even have to call for tenders. The hon. member for Simcoe told us about the expenditure of a general grant for dredging; but there at least tenders were supposed to be called for. But here the Minister of Railways is not even supposed to call for tenders, and he proposes legislation in the most vicious form known in order to get political support. Wherever a by-election comes on, he can appropriate a portion of this road money, and put it into 'the hands of his political friends, and they will say to the electors: Now you vote right and you will get so much. They will go further than that and they will say: You will not get this grant until the election is over, and if the election does not go right, you will not get the money at all. I "am only pointing out what they are doing in New Brunswick, and I am pointing "out what they will do all over this country, if this legislation goes through. Therefore, I say it is a piece of vicious legislation, and ought not to be passed.

Under the Ontario system the initiative was left with the counties. The county passed a by-law and adopted _ the system and the government had to ' contribute a portion of the cost of the road to the county. If this government gave the money to the provinces then the provinces could increase the sum to the counties and still leave the initiative with the counties. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Kent is a very good one. The people should be interested and the initiative should be left with the counties.

I asked the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Borden) in the few remarks I made a few minutes ago, to explain to the committee whether he understood the effect of clause 6, to mean that the federal government were to enter practically into the business of looking after the roads of the country. That, I submit, would be the effect of the section because it would give them the power to do so. The right hon. gentleman stated that this was intended to apply to a case where, for instance, a province did not have an adequate system in regard to the expenditure of its road money, under which circumstances the government could
go in and expend the whole of the money that was appropriated for that province itself. That answer is not a satisfactory one because it is not to be supposed that any province would consider itself as not having an adequate i system for spending troad moneys and it would not therefore give to the federal government an opportunity of making that expenditure. The right hon. gentleman has given no reason why the government should enter into the arena of provincial powers and engage in the task of looking after the roads of the country. He was good enough to say to the hon. member for Kent, who made a very practical suggestion as to the utilization of the road money generally, which mean1, nothing more nor less than a suggestion that we had previously made, that the wisdom of the expenditure of roil mom/ depended on the unification of the authoi ity so that the roads would get the bem'fit cf the assistance that came from the di'iyrent quarters. If that was the proposal that came before the government it can never be worked out under section 6. It would be impossible to work conjointly with the provinces or with the municipalities along the lines proposed here. Manifestly the Minister of Railways and Canals has not the equipment in his department to deal with roads at all. Before the minister could pass judgment upon the question as to whether the roads system of any province was good or not, or the engineering facilities and equipment of the province were such as that the country could expect a wise and prudent expenditure of the road money entrusted to him, the minister would need to gather around him a very large staff of specialists on that subject, not a staff which would be adequate for any particular province, but a staff greater and more numerous than that which they have in any province to-day. The minister would need to have such a staff before he could safely expend a dollar of the money that was put in his hands for better roads. Are we going to originate a system of that kind? The government disclaim any such idea. Still, they have power to do it at any time and, as my hon. friend from. Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) has pointed out, evil results will follow from it. My right hon. friend said, with regard to the constitutional difficulties that were suggested the other day, that no province would object to the federal government giving them money, or spending money in the province, and that therefore there was no constitutional obstacle. Well, the fathers of confederation, fifty years ago, said that it was a wise and prudent thing for Canada that the provincial governments should look after the roads of the country. Having regard to that distribution of power they said: We will provide the provinces with funds from the

central treasury in order that they may look alter the roads of the country. They have been doing it for fifty years. This government say that they propose to continue that system by giving additional aid, yet they put in the Bill a power which will nullify the rest of it and endanger the constitutional system adopted fifty years ago. It certainly will dislocate the system under which municipalities all over the country, look after the repair of the roads because it will nullify the system of statute labour. I submit that this is not a wise measure and I would therefore move, seconded by Mr. Proulx, that the clause be struck out.
Amendment negatived (Yeas 48, nays 52.).

would like to draw the attention of the government to the need of an armoury in the city of Moosejaw. I want, for the benefit of the Prime Minister, to read certain correspondence which has passed between the city of Moosejaw and the government, or rather the Minister of Militia and Defence. The following is a letter addressed to the Hon. Colonel Hughes by Mr. W. F. Heale, city clerk of Moosejaw:
Honourable Colonel Hughes,
Minister of Militia and Defence,
Ottawa.
Sir,-I am instructed by the Moosejaw City Council to communicate with your department re the delay in bringing the armouries on the Fairford Street site. The following resolution was passed by the council at their meeting held on January 8th and I am instructed to forward it to you with the request that you kindly deal with the matter as early as possible.
That the council very much regret that no move has been made to construct the armouries so long promised, .and that the Minister of Militia and Defence be requested to state as early as possible the intention of his department in this connection, as the council are desirous of using this very valuable site for other purposes unless used by the department .without further delay.
I am. Sir,
Your obedient servant,
W. F. HEALE, City Clerk.
A reply was made to that letter, and it is to that reply that I ask the very particular attention of the Prime Minister. This is it:
Minister's office,
Ottawa, February 1, 1912.
Re Drill Shed.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of January 10th, 1912, with the 4 instructions ' from your city council re ' the delay in building the armouries on the Fair-ford street site.'
I do not understand what your letter means. Nor can I comprehend what you mean by your use of the word ' delay.' Nor can I imagine what your reference is about the 4 armouries so long promised.'
I have been Minister of Militia since October, and am responsible for no promise made before that time. Will you permit me to say that I think it would be muoh better ta9te on the part of your council, instead of passing a resolution of regret and fault-finding, to have quietly made a request and placed the facts before me.
Your fault-finding letter is the first intimation I have had officially that there is such a place as Moosejaw or that you want an armoury. While in the west, I met a number of splendid fellows from Moosejaw, officers and others, who spoke to me like gentlemen on this matter, and I promised them, and have carried out my promises, to recommend a sum of money, not for an armoury, which is of no use for a large and growing place like Moosejaw, but for a drill hall and armouries.
I also suggested the formation of a city corps for Moosejaw.
Might I suggest that as 

our council seems to go about it in a blundering sort of fashion that they should appoint some of those gentlemen whom I had the privilege of meeting in the west to carry on the negotiations1 in the matter? They seemed to know their business and were very judicious.
If it were left to them, I think Moosejaw would soon have a splendid drill hall and armouries attached and would also have a city regiment.	[DOT]
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) SAM HUGHES.
City Clerk,
W.F. Heale, Esq.,
Moosejaw.
I wish to say that the property offered by the city of Moosejaw had been accepted by the government, but there was a slight cloud on the title, the circumstances being that the prior holders of the title had passed it over to the city as part of a park, and in the deed to the city it is stated that it must not be used for commercial purposes, and must not be alienated. The city of Moosejaw naturally can only give the same kind of title to the government that they themselvesi have, and I understand that between the Department of Public Works, the Department of Militia and the Department of Justice who are mixed up in it, there is delay because of this. In reference to the answer given to the city of Moosejaw by the Minister of Militia, without saying anything offensive to the Minister of Militia, I deem the letter he wrote to be unworthy of the high and dignified position that he for the moment holds.

The hon. member did not do me the honour of sending me word that he w.as going to bring this matter up to-day, or I would have been in my place in the House when he began his remarks. I may inform him that the negotiations in reference to the mat-

ter to which he has referred have been handed over to the Moosejaw Board of Trade, the city council being too hidebound a Grit institution to treat any one with proper courtesy. This action has had this effect: The city council of Moosejaw, having been relieved of the necessity of sending letters of a blustering and threatening description, the matter is working out very nicely. ' I think the minister is in error. They never said they would alienate the property. They would use it for other purposes.

The city may use it for public purposes, but it cannot sell it to any one. These gentlemen talk as if they owned the property and were giving us a $40,000 site. However, the matter is proceeding very nicely now. The Moosejaw council has come to its senses, and the board of trade is dealing with the matter.

If not, Friday might be agreeable to both of us. If the hon. gentleman intends to press it to a vote, he might let it go over to Monday or Tuesday of next week.

The conditions which the resolution takes notice of are urgent, and, as my hon. friend has said, many things are happening and I would wish to have this matter considered before the condition to which it relates has passed out of existence by effluxion of time. Well, my hon. friend can go on.

Mr. Speaker, it is my purpose to call attention as strongly as I can to the condition of affairs which exists today in the western provinces, and which is generally spoken of as the grain blockade. I do not suppose it will be necessary for me to spend any serious length of time in demonstrating that there is such a blockade. About the time this notice was given the leading newspaper of the west took measures to inquire into the conditions as they then existed. That paper wired on January 29 to 150 points. At the time notice was given of this resolution it had heard from 49 points, and at only nine of them was it reported that there was no blockade.
I will not trouble the House with any long list of the facts as shown by the newspaper mentioned, the ' Free Press.' They are, I have no doubt, within the knowledge of many members of the House. But here is one instance, the very first one I took down. The wire is from Quill Lake, Saskatchewan. There were 52 orders or cars. A car was ordered on November 9, which was placed on January 23, and 50 per cent of the grain was still in the farmers' hands. At Foam Lake, Saskatchewan, there were 60 orders on the order book, the elevators were full, there were
100.000	bushels in the farmers' hands, and
50.000	bushels threshed. Other members
of the House will, no doubt, give the committee further information as to the existence of the blockade. But it may be of interest to give some facts as to why there is a blockade, and why that blockade should be of such an extraordinary character and at such an extraordinary time of the year as this information establishes it to be. A blockade is the condition in which grain is offered for sale beyond the quantity that can be, or is being, transported to market. In every year there is shortly after the beginning of threshing, and before the close of navigation, in the nature of things, if the markets are good, necessarily a rush of grain, and a car shortage, or a blockade, or a partial blockade, during that period of the year is something that has occurred frequently, and may be looked for to occur in the future on many occasions.	Last year it did not occur.
The year before it did occur, and so on from year to year, as the occasion was, the blockade existed or did not exist. But this yfear the conditions were extraordinary. In the first place the acreage under crop was much larger than it ever was before. In the next place the crop, so far as its growth was concerned, was probably generally heavier than it ever was before in the history of the country. Over and above that, the season was unfavourable for harvesting, and the harvesting
did not begin as early as usual. When the work of transporting the crop to thle lake front began, it began later than usual, and the result has been that from the time transportation of the crop to the lake front began until thie present time, there has been a condition of grain blockade. Under ordinary circumstances the car shortage or blockade that would exist between the beginning of the transportation of the crop and the close of navigation, would be to some .extent practically eliminated after the close of navigation. The rush to get the grain forward would stop at that period, and the gradual movement of grain out of the terminal elevators by the all-rail route to the seaboard, and the gradual coming forward of the grain, would militate against a condition of car shortage or grain blockade shortly after the close of navigation.
This season the condition is that instead of the close of navigation marking a finish of the grain blockade, it was after the close of navigation that the grain blockade became more acute than before, and that the damage to the business interests of the country resulted more strongly than before. The conditions have been aggravated by the fact that, owing to the bad weather of last fall, it is practically impossible to get all the grain threshed, and a great deal of the grain that has been threshed was in a damp condition at that time, and having been placed in storage, in the farmers' granary or in a country elevator; has become liable to destruction, because of being heated as the result of its being damp when it was stored. So that we are in the face of a condition which not only operates against the price which the farmer received for his grain, but that tends to the actual destruction of a considerable part of the total crop of the northwest by reason of the blockade.
Have you any definite, or fairly definite, information as to what percentage of the grain has not been threshed as yet, and what percentage is in a damp condition and likely to be destroyed?

The most definite information that I can give is the representation of the manager of the Ogilvie Milling Company, who reports that there are 30,000,000 bushels of damaged wheat in the west unfit for milling, and about that amount was unthreshed in the middle of January. This is the condition as it exists at the present time. With a larger crop than we ever had before, and with that crop in danger of being destroyed to a considerable extent, because it is not going forward, we have a more extraordinary condition of grain blockade than ever before existed in the northwest. Just as

to the magnitude of the damage, I will not say the disaster, to the interests of the country let me give the figures as. to the amount of grain that has to be handled. I take the estimate of Sir Byron Walker as placed before the directors of the Bank of Commerce at their annual meeting. He estimates the total yield as 400,000,000 bushels ef grain, of which 175,000,000 bushels are wheat, 180,000,000 oats., 35,000,000 barley, and 6,000,000 flax, and he values this crop at $200,000,000. He also states that the crop of wheat was expected at one time to be 200,000,000 or 225,000,000 of bushels, so that the condition is that the farmer of the west who-by reason of the area that he had sown, by reason of the expenditure that he had incurred, by reason of the conditions that prevailed in the early part of the growing season-had reason to expect 200,000,000 or 225,000,000 bushels of wheat, has only, as a matter of fact, secured 175,000,000 bushels. That is to say by reason of the unfavourable season the farmer is short, according to Sir Byron Walker, between 25,000,000 and
50.000.	000 bushels of his reasonable expectation.
And let it he remembered that these expectations are not pencil and paper estimates, but are based upon the expenditure that the farmer has incurred. He has ploughed his land, he has sown his seed, he has maintained his help and, having incurred all these expenses, he might reasonably have expected results aggregating
200.000.	000 or 225,000,000 bushels. But, notwithstanding these expenditures on his part, he has secured only 175,000,000 bushels. That is, he is between 25,000,000 and
50.000.	000 bushels short of his reasonable expectations of the result of his investment, the shortage being due to the unfavourable conditions of the harvest season.
Does that include the three western provinces?

I assume that it does. I am merely giving the House Sir Byron Walker's statement, which, I understand, covers the three western provinces. And I know of no place where I could get a more complete, comprehensive and, i presume, accurate statement.
That result might follow great drought as well as too much rain.

Certainly. I am merely giving the facts Sir Byron Walker has stated. My hon. friend need not be alarmed; these facts have only an indirect bearing on the argument I wish to make. Of the movement of this crop, Mr. Thompson, of the Ogilvie Mills, estimates that there were 100,000,000 bushels of wheat marketed by January 11. Estimating that 25,000,000 bushels would be needed for seed Mr. OLIVER.
and bread, that would mean 50,000,000 bushels of wheat still to he marketed on January 10. Then, as I have already said in answer to the bon. member's inquiry, the same authority estimates that there was from 25,000,000 to 30,000,000 bushels of wheat still in the farmers' hands at that time much of it unthreshed, most of it damp, and all of it unfit for milling. As to the grain going forward, there was inspected at Winnipeg up to January 10, of wheat 67,000,000 bushels, of oats 17,500,000 bushels, of barley 250,000 bushels, of flax 250,000 bushels. So that, of 100,000,000 bushels of wheat marketed up to January 10, only 67,000,000 bushels had reached Winnipeg up to that time.
Deliveries began about September 10. Owing to unfavourable conditions of weather, the deliveries were not very strong at first. About November 10 the blockade became acute and continued until the close of navigation.	It was expected that at the close of navigation the blockade would be to some extent relieved. But, contrary to common expectations and the experience of previous seasons, the blockade has been more acute, not less acute, since the close _ of navigation. At the close of navigation there was 6,000,000 bushels of wheat in store at the terminal elevators. At last account there was 18,000,000 bushels in store at terminal elevators at Fort William, and these elevators were full. The total capacity of the elevators is, of course, much greater than the figure I have given; but, owing to the great number of grades this season and to the damaged crop, the actual capacity of the elevators is reduced to this extent. So, we have this condition: A blockade beginning on September 10th which continued until the close of navigation, and which after the close of navigation became more acute, and continued to January 10th, the date I have mentioned. Of the 100,000,000 bushels of wheat marketed -according to Mr. Thompson's statement -up to January 10th, at least half must have been marketed under blockade conditions. That is the season began on September 10th. We will assume that there was no blockade until November 10th. Two months marketing, free of blockade up to November 10th, and from that date to January 10th two months of actual blockade. Therefore, it is fair to assume that if we had 50,000,000 bushels marketed free of blockade, we must have had the other 50,000,000 bushels marketed during the blockade. So, whatever loss would occur from blockade conditions would have to be suffered on not less than 50,000,000 bushels.
When I gave notice of this motion, the terminal elevators were full of grain, and no matter what the world's market price might be, the grain in the farmer's hands

must remain in his hands. It could not be stored in country elevators, for the country elevators were full; the country elevators could not empty into the terminal elevators because the terminal elevators were full; and apparently it was not possible to transport the grain from the terminal elevator to the eastern seaboard at a rate that would give any substantial relief to the condition of blockade existing. I have here a despatch appearing in the Winnipeg '(Free IPrefcs;' of January 25, which states the condition in regard to the elevators at Fort William:
There were in the Fort William books last night 3,577 cars on order not loaded

That is, ears ordered for eastern shipment.
-representing over 4,326,500 bushels of grain of all kinds; and for over three weeks there has never been less than 3,000 oars on order, but not loaded.
