at the close of navigation, conditions settle. The grain goes into storage, it is not forwarded as rapidly, some relief is given by transportation eastward, and, generally speaking, the condition of blockade ceases at or soon after the close of navigation. But, in the case of this season, instead of the expectation of relief being realised, the condition of blockade was made permanent and was accentuated. While there was a reasonable reflex on the farmer in his price because of the blockade condition existing before December 10, after December 10 a panic condition ensued and panic prices became the rule to the farmer. Instead of the country operator paying the farmer the winter price subject to the reduction that I have made for storage, insurance and other charges, being faced with the possibility that he could not get the grain forwarded at all, or did not know when he could get it forwarded panic prices resulted to the farmer, panic conditions prevailed and have prevailed ever since.
I have already said that unless the damaged grain gets to the hospital elevator by the first of April it is, in all probability, destroyed. This fact, of course, accentuates the panic condition that prevails this season. Of course, all figures must be estimates, actual accuracy cannot be demonstrated, but the figures which I propose to give the committee are unquestionably within the mark. On the 50,000,000 bushels of grain marketed between November 10 and January 10-that is marketed between the first blockade condition and January 10 when the blockade condition was demonstrated to be impossible of relief-estimating the loss to the farmers at six cents a bushel, the loss to the farmers would be $3,000,000. But, on the 50,000,000 bushels remaining to be marketed after J anuary 10, and, which, according to the statement of Mr. Thompson of the Ogilvie Milling Company, must be marketed under panic conditions, I think it is a very moderate estimate to say that the loss would be ten cents a bushel to the farmers, or a loss of $5,000,000 from January 10 to the end of the season and of $3,000,000 from the beginning of the blockade on November 10 to January 10.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that 50,000,000 bushels was the amount of wheat in the farmers hands on January 10?
Yes.

I presume that the hon. gentleman must know that it has never been the custom of the western farmers to ship all their grain out, but that- a great deal of the grain is kept over until the following summer and that it would

not have been shipped if there had been ever so many cars.

I have already said to the committee that the fact of so much of the grain being damp, makes it necessary that the grain shall be got forward to the drying or hospital elevators, or it will go out of condition. It will be seriously damaged or altogether destroyed. The conditions this season differ from ordinary conditions.

What percentage of this
50,000,000 bushels was damaged?

I have the statement of Mr. Thompson, of the Ogilvie Milling Company, and also of a Mr. Black, I think- at any rate of two gentlemen connected with the Ogilvie Milling Company-both estimating that 30,000,000 bushels will be remaining in the farmers' hands or damaged by reason of being damp, a large part of it unthreshed at that time, and a considerable part of it is unthreshed yet. My hon. friends, _ who are acquainted with farming conditions, know that if grain in the stook when the snow comes on, is threshed, that grain must get to where it will be dried before the hot weather comes on, because, otherwise it would be very much damaged.
It is not threshed yet, is it?

A great deal of it is not threshed. When a blockade exists, and it becomes impossible for either the farmer or the dealer to get the grain forwarded, then certainly the grain is safer in the stook than it is in the farmers' granary or in the country elevator.
There is no doubt that there is a great deal of grain to-day remaining unthreshed in the stooks, that if there was no blockade would have been threshed and gone forward, and the farmer would have got the money for it.
How does the hon. gentleman make that out?
My hon. friend (Mr. Staples) lives in a farming constituency, and he knows perfectly well that what I am saying is correct, and there is m use arguing it between us.

I am only asking the hon. gentleman for information. I am proud to say I am a farmer and have a fair knowledge of what takes place amongst the farming community, and I can state that every available threshing machine has been working overtime trying to get the grain threshed.

Well, I am not disputing that at all. I have said that there is a great deal of the grain still unthreshed, 128
and I have said that in my judgment it is more than likely that a great deal of that grain would have been threshed if there had been no blockade.. But, there being a blockade, there was no object in threshing it when it would have suffered greater damage after being threshed than it was suffering by remaining in the stooks, when it was not possible to get it forwarded properly.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that the threshing machines in the west have been idle instead of operating?
I mean in some cases they have undoubtedly.
I can assure you they have not.

My hon. friend (Mr. Staples) is no doubt familiar with the constituency he represents, but the conditions in that constituency, as the House knows, are not the same as they are in other parts of the west.
I have a fair knowledge of the whole west.

Then my hon. friend will have to allow us who represent other parts of the west to speak for our own constituencies just as we will be glad to have the hon. gentleman speak for the part of the west he represents.
Then I understand the hon. gentleman to say that in the part of the west he represents the threshing machines have been idle.

Yes, at some parts of the year undoubtedly. I was giving the House an estimate, a conservative estimate I believe, of the direct loss to the farmer as the result of the blockade conditions. I got as far as the estimated loss on wheat, but I wish to add that in my judgment it is reasonable to consider that on oats, barley and flax, which are subject to the same blockade conditions, there would be a loss of no less than two million dollars. My estimate is that on wheat, oats, barley and flax, and because of the depreciation in price to the farmers resulting from blockade conditions in this season the farmers have suffered a loss of not less than ten million dollars.

The hon. gentleman stated that there was a loss of five million dollars on wheat, taking fifty million bushels at ten cents a bushel, but a moment afterwards' the hon. gentleman admitted that there were about thirty million bushels of this which was damaged and it would necessarily be forced to go forward, and, as we know, it is the custom of the farmers to hold a large quantity over. So, I think,



if he is fair in_his estimate, it would be right to cut his five million bushels down to at least three million bushels. We want to have as fair an estimate as we can.

I want to say to my hon. friend and to the House generally that I have made this estimate as moderate as in my judgment the circumstances will admit in accordance with truth. When my hon. friend suggests that we have thirty million bushels of damaged grain which must go forward or be lost, and which cannot go forward by reason of the blockade, he surely must also admit that my estimate is below the mark rather than above it. But I want to dwell a little on this point of the damaged grain and the liability of the total destruction of that grain. I have only dealt with the loss that is accruing to-day, and it is a very moderate estimate of the loss that I have given on the grain that is going forward; that is, the grain upon which the commercial value is not altogether destroyed. But there is no doubt that there is a large part of the grain crop-and the evidence of Mr. Thompson and of Mr. Black and the evidence of the sense of any man who has travelled in the west this -winter shows it, there is a large part of the grain crop that stands in danger of total destruction. To repeat: every man knows that when wheat is threshed in a damp condition, when that wheat is stored as it must be stored, unless it is dry before being stored it is bound to heat and if it heats its commercial value will either be destroyed or be depreciated to such an extent as to be a very great loss. That is the condition we are face to face with. Remember, I have shown that on the statement made as to the possibility of transportation out of the terminal elevators there must be left in the farmers' hands anywhere from thirteen million bushels to eighteen million Ibushels of wheat until April 1st.
Can they not feed that wheat to anything?

If they had something to feed it to they could-well, perhaps I had better stick to the subject. I was going to make a remark about certain classes of live stock that might be used to feed the wheat to if we had our farms near Peterborough, hut I won't. I said, Mr Speaker that on Mr. Thompson's estimate there were thirty million bushels unfit for milling, on Mr. Black's estimate there were thirty million bushels unthreshed at the time he made the estimate, and I say that if the damaged grain is not in the hospital by April 1, its value will be either altogether or largely destroyed. The farmers have been advised Mr. STEVENS.
to build granaries; the farmers have been advised to do a great many things, but I want to say to the House that the farmers' granary does not meet this case. Let the farmer have as fine a, granary as he may please, if he stores that grain in it that grain will be damaged or destroyed and the same exactly applies in the case of a country elevator which has no drying facilities. The damaged grain must get forward to the drying plant before 'the warm weather sets in or it will be lost. I am assuming that out of the thirty millions that are said to be unthreshed there is a possible loss of fifteen million bushels. If the value of that is estimated at forty cents a bushel to the farmer-because understand it is damaged grain and not grain of full value-that would be a loss of six million dollars. I want to impress upon the House and upon the Government the contingency which they are face to face with in this case. I therefore estimate the unavoidable loss to the farmers from shortage of crop and from damage to grain in this season at thirty-five million dollars, or one-third of the total value of their wheat crop. _
But if he is to lose $10,000,000 by reason of the grain blockade-and any man who is interested in either the growing or marketing of grain will say that he is going to lose a great deal more-and if on top of that, he is to lose $6,000,000 by reason of damaged grain, his loss will he on account of unavoidable causes, $35,000,000, and on account of avoidable causes, $16,000,000; a total of $51,000,000, or one-half of the total value of his crop. We have heard that the west is a rich country and that the people there are optimistic and recover from a condition of difficulty very easily; and it is pointed out to us that parts of that country have been settled for 30 years, and that the farmers should be in a condition to take care of their crop, and should not be in such a condition as to have no place to store it safely when it is out of condition. Let me remind the House that 150,000 homesteads have been taken in the four years from 1908 to 1911, as many as were taken in the years from 1875 to 1903. That is, there were as many homesteads taken in the western provinces in the last four years as were taken in the 28 years which ended in 1903. That is to say, we have as many absolutely new settlers in the country as we had old settlers between those dates. It is a necessary condition of the rapid expansion of settlement in that country that there must always be, so long as that rapid expansion continues, a very large proportion of people who are only in the beginning of establishing themselves who are not by any possibility in a position to protect themselves on such an occasion as the present season. It is well, I

think, that the House and the country should understand that at least one-third of the homesteading population of that country, have come there within the past three years; and let it be remembered that it is on the new settler, who is not well fitted with buildings and equipment, who is farthest from the railroad and therefore, under the greatest disabilities, that the bulk of the loss falls. I want to impress upon the House the serious damage that is being done to the progress of that country by reason of the losses that are being suffered this year.
It is not only the settler who suffers loss. The farmer buys largely on credit, and the storekeeper sells when he knows that the farmer has no money. They all expect to get their money out of the crop. So that the store bills, and all other bills and notes' mature in November or December; and when the whole business of the country depends upon the collection of the year's accounts in either of these months, and the accounts cannot be collected, because the grain has not been marketed, although it has been grown, there is a disarrangement of the business of the country, which is damaging to its every interest. The damage is not confined to the farmer; it spreads into every line_ of business. Cases have come to my notice, and I have no doubt to the notice of many other members of the -House, of not only farmers, but business men who have been actually put out of business by reason of the grain blockade this year. Farmers and business men who were doing the best they could, and would have succeeded, even in the face of the unfortunate weather conditions that prevailed; have been put out of business absolutely because the money that the crop was worth, could not be realized because of this blockade.
As the resolution which I have placed before the House mentions, action has been taken by the government to give some measure of relief. The railway companies have been consulted, and I presume, in response to suggestion or pressure by the government, have made certain arrangements which will result in their being able to give transportation to elevator accommodation by shorter hauls Jhan up to the present time exist. I have inquired into the measure of relief that has been proposed, and I desire to give to the House some of the particulars. The Canadian Pacific railway has issued a rate sheet on wheat and oats to Minneapolis and Duluth, giving the same rate of freight to those points as to Fort William. This rate became effective on February 16, and it expires on April 30. It is effective for 74 days. But 34 days expired between the date of the issue of the rate sheet, and the date of its coming into effect, and 67 days expired between the close of navigation and the com-1261
ing into effect of this rate. This rate applies only to the province of Saskatchewan and only to grain for export.
The Canadian Northern railway have given a rate on wheat to Duluth and it is also the^ same rate as to Fort William, which applies only on shipments in transit in bond through the tjnited States for exports. It was approved by the Interstate Commerce Commission on January 20, 1912, and_ became effective on January 29. It expires on April 30, and will be in force 91 days. It became effective 49 days after the close of navigation, and was effective 9 days after it was approved by the Interstate Commerce Commission. The Canadian Pacific railway also gave a rate on barley and flax to Minneapolis. This rate was issued on December 20, 1911, and became effective on January 23, 1912. It expires on April 30, and is effective 98 days. It became effective 43 days after navigation closed, and 34 days expired between the date of its issue and the date of its coming into effect. This rate on barley and flax is not the Fort William rate. It is 4 cents higher per 100 pounds than the Fort William rate, ion barley and flax from Manitoba, and 9 cents per 100 pounds higher than the Fort William rate on barley and flax from Saskatchewan. The difference is practically 2 cents a bushel for barley and flax in Manitoba, and 41 cents a bushel in Saskatchewan. I want to give the House some facts in regard to the possibilities of the marketing of barley under this arrangement. Because it will be observed, Ijhat "while the wheat rate is only, for bonding in transit, the barley and flax rate is for consumption in the United States, and so it is interesting to us to know if there is any market for barley for consumption in the United States. I have here a statement in regard to a car of feed barley shipped from Carman, Manitoba, to Minneapolis, on December 8, 1911. The car contained 1,253 06 bushels, and was sold at Minneapolis at $1.07 a bushel realizing $1,340.84. ' That is to say less freight charges $72.53, customs entry charges $1.20, weighing charges 40 cents, switching charges $1.50, commission in Minneapolis $12.53, commission in Winnipeg $12.53, total $100.69; net proceeds of the car in Minneapolis $1,240.15. The Fort William price was 50 cents a bushel, the Minneapolis price was $1.07 a bushel. The Minneapolis net price, that is less the expenses I have mentioned was 99 cents a bushel.
What was the duty?
The duty was 30 cents a bushel,: and the Minneapolis net price less duty, was 69 cents a bushel. The value of the car at Fort William was. $626.54, and the net value of the car at Minneapolis was
If these figures are accurate, and I presume the hon. gentleman thinks they are, does it not seem reasonable that the farmers would ship all their barley to the United States and pay the duty?

I think they are going to ship a very large proportion of it there once they get the freight rates. But the rates that applied on that car were rates on the Great Northern which has always had a through rate to Minneapolis. Points on the other two railway systems did not have through rates to Minneapolis until this arrangement was entered into which became effective on the 23rd of January. Since that rate became effective there is no doubt that very large shipments have been taking place, and that the congestion or grade blockade has been relieved to some extent by that means.
But what I want, to draw your attention to, is the paragraph in the resolution which I have placed before the House which asks the government to make such arrangement, or to urge such arrangement, as will give the same rate on barley and flax to Minneapolis as to Fort William. On the barley that is now being shipped to Minneapolis the farmer pays two cents a bushel more than if it were shipped to Fort William, if it is from Manitoba, and 44 cents a bushel more than if it is shipped from Saskatchewan. That makes a difference of $25 a car on barley from Manitoba, and $56 a car on barley from Saskatchewan. The barley crop is estimated at 35 millions of bushels the flax crop at 6 millions of bushels. I find from the returns from the Trade and Commerce Department that 2 million bushels of barley, and 2 million bushels of flax have been received at Fort William between September 1st and December 21st. If 2 million bushels of that grain came from Manitoba, and 2 million bushels from Saskatchewan, it means that the farmers have had to pay $130,000 more upon that barley and flax in order to get the advantage of the Minneapolis market. I want to impress upon the government there is no reason, there is no justice, in making that discrimination in these rates; that if they are going to give an outlet to the western farmer who grows barley and flax, if the railroads can afford to haul wheat at the same rate to Minneapolis and Duluth as to Fort William, they can afford to haul the barley and flak at the same rate, and the

farmer should not be required to pay that 2 cents a bushel from Manitoba, and 44 cents a bushel from Saskatchewan for the privilege of getting the benefit of the Minneapolis market after paying the duty as well.
I have given the House the informa-do in order to relieve the conditions of which we have complained. Now I want to draw attention to what they might have done in order to relieve those conditions and to demonstrate how very far short they have fallen of even measurably attempting to meet these requirements. I have pointed out that the panic condition which exists to-day in the west is the consequence of the blockade in the terminal elevators.
And the reason for the continuance of the blockade in the terminal elevators is that the railway company, or companies are not able to forward the grain fast enough to the ocean port to relieve that situation. The only remedy is to find a shorter outlet. The outlet in such a case is any placS that will take the grain; and Minneapolis and Duluth are the places which are able to store the grain and are able to mill and market such of the grain as is fit for milling and marketing. As to the effort to relieve the grain blockade, let us consider a few figures. The length of haul from Winnipeg to St. Paul is 462 miles, as compared with a haul from Winnipeg to St. John of 2,178 miles-four and a half times the distance. From Moosejaw to St. Paul is 738 miles, and from Moose-jaw to St. John 2,571 miles, or three and a half times as far. From Calgary to St. Paul is 1,166 miles, and from Calgary to St. John 2,979 miles, or two and a half times as far. By taking measures which will enable the grain marketed within a radius of Winnipeg to be sent to St. Paul instead of to St. John, the capacity of the rolling stock of the railway is practically increased four and a half fold. That is if they have been able to carry 10,000,000 bushels from Winnipeg to St. John, they would have been able to carry 50,000,000 bushels in the same time from Winnipeg to St. Paul. It is obvious that there was a means of preventing the blockade, a means of breaking the blockade, but the means were not taken in time to do the work. Let me point out that if my hon. friend (Mr. Foster), had taken in time the measures which he proposes to take-I understand from the press-there would have been no blockade and the losses that have been suffered1 would not have been suffered;. If the rates and conditions which, I understand, it is proposed to put into effect on Maroh 7, had been put into effect on November 10, when a condition of blockade actually existed, not in expectation but in fact, the Canadian Pacific

railway wheat rate would have been 98 days longer; the Canadian Northern railway wheat rate 74 days longer, and1 the Canadian Pacific railway rate 74 days longer. On the average there would have been twice as 'long a time in which to deliver this grain and reduce the blockade. But although these special rates are allowed until April 30, again I submit to the committee that the month of April may be counted out so far as the transport of damaged grain is concerned with any result of saving its full value. If the period of transportation at the rates that came into effect on the date I have mentioned are taken with that month of April deducted, as it must be, the Canadian Pacific railway are giving the wheat rate for 44 effective days, the Canadian Northern railway for 61 effective days, and the Canadian Pacific railway on barley for 68 effective days. I claim on behalf of the people of the west that measures should have been taken to have these rates brought into effect at any rate as soon as the condition of blockade existed, and that had that action been taken the blockade, which had begun, would have been relieved and the country would have been many millions of dollars better off than it is going to be to-day.
To what purpose did my hon. friend take pleasures with the railway companies in this direction? Was it to relieve the situation for the farmer? If it was, then he certainly did not take measures as he should have done. Why did he restrict the operation of the rate on wheat and oats over the Canadian Pacific railway to the province of Saskatchewan? Why were the rates on barley and flax made higher than the corresponding rates on wheat and oats? Why were not these rates secured at an earlier date? Was it because he and the railway men came together and said: Thgre is so much storage in Minneapolis and Duluth and we will reduce these rates low enough to enable us to haul the grain that will fill that storage, and if we do that the rest of the grain can wait our convenience to haul it out as it best suits us? For what other reason could it have been that my hon. friend secured the regulations with these restrictions? Does he say that it was because the Interstate Commerce Commission would not give permission sooner? All I can say is that all he had to do was to ask the Interstate Commerce Commission sooner and he would have got the permission that much sooner. There is no possibility of laying the blame anywhere except on the shoulders of my hon. friend and of the government of which he is a prominent member. I find a reference to the despatches in the press that the Interstate Commerce Commission did not put any bar of lapse of time in the way of notice of the going into effect to these rates. The following despatch appeared in the Winnipeg 'Free Press' of January 22:
Washington, D.C., January 21.-The United States laws require 'thirty days' notice, and the commission never grants permission to establish rates on less time except under extraordinary emergencies. The commission's invariable policy is never to grant permission to establish rate9 on grain because it is such a sensitive proposition, inasmuch as a slight disturbance of a rate line of adjustment at any given point throws the whole matter out of gear.
In these cases it was represented to the commission that grain at certain Canadian points was damp and spoiling. The rates of Canadian carriers have hitherto been made to Fort William and Port Arthur, but storage capacity at these places has been entirely exhausted, and was so inadequate that it was desired to establish these new rate9 to United States points only for storage, drying &c., while in transit in bond through the United States for export only.
Now, in face of that fact, I want to draw the attention of the House to the rate sheet issued by the Canadian Pacific railway on the 12th of January 1912, giving rates on carloads from stations in the western provinces. It became effective on the 16th day of February, 1912. I presume that this rate sheet had the approval of the commission before it was issued; if so, I ask what excuse was there for not giving effect to that rate before the 16th of February. In the case of barley and flaxseed, the rate issued on the 20th December became effective on the 23rd of January. In the case of the Canadian Northern railway, for some reason or other, there was not the same interval between the issue of the rate sheet and its coming into effect. The Inter-state Commerce Commission gave permission, and in nine days afterwards the rate became effective. I think it is demonstrated that the delay that has occurred in bringing these rates into effect is not due to the Inter-state Commerce Commission, it is due to the arrangement entered into between my hon. friend and the Canadian railway companies, and I want to insist that that arrangement was entered into for the benefit of the railway companies instead of the benefit of the farmers. If not, why these restrictions? Why not open the door, if it had to be opened, as soon as' possible and as widely as possible? My hon. friend must have known that the conditions were as I have stated. He has under his control the machinery of the Grain Act, he has officers in touch with the grain situation throughout the west, there clould not be a grain blockade in the western country without his having knowledge of it. I say, therefore, that when he has taken action at all he is condemned be-

cause he did not, take action in time to be effective. To make it sure that the government had knowledge of these conditions, I read the report of E. D. Eddy,
B.S.A., published by the Department of Agriculture under date of Ottawa, January 12. This report deals with the crop and climatic conditions throughout the west, it is a part of the public service for which this country pays, and the government not only had it in their hands, but it is their statement for which they are responsible. This report says:
The climatic conditions prevailing throughout the prairie provinces of Canada were very abnormal during the season of 1911. Seeding was largely done about the usual time, from the middle of April to the middle of May and under favourable conditions. During the latter part of May and June the conditions were favourable, with sufficient rain in most parts and reasonably warm weather. July was cloudy, showery and cool, growth being rapid and almost rank, but toward the end of the month rust appeared in some parts and there was little sign of ripening. During August unseasonably cold weather prevailed, preventing ripening, rust became prevalent in some districts, and frost occurred from August 22 to Aug 28 doing great damage. During September the weather was generally cold and wet with heavy damage resulting to the crops from frost and rust. Damaging frosts occurred in many districts on September 6, 8, 21 and 25. During the first part of October the weather was moderately dry and warm, but owing to rust and the abundant supply of moisture crops refused to ripen. The freeze up came on October 25, or three weeks earlier than usual. Much cutting still remained to be done, and as the stocks were wet from recent rains considerable injury resulted to even fairly well matured grain which was in etook. The latter part of October was cold, and on November 1st the temperature dropped to 6 below zero. On November 4th something very unusual in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, after tho freeze up, happened; the weather suddenly turned warm and rain fell all day. This was followed on November 8 with from 3 to a inches of snow and on November 10, 20 below zero was registered. The snow and extreme cold in November came when a large proportion of the threshing remained to be done. December was remarkably fair and mild and the threshing was continued, but the grain that was in stock is very tough and. a large proportion of it unmarketable.
With these facts in hand, with the knowledge of the conditions that must have come to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I again ask what excuse has he to offer for failing to take the action that lay before him from the beginning of the season?	When he did take action
why did he not take effective action? I have asked	a question, and I
propose to give to the House the answer that appears to be correct. I think a large part of the answer may be found in a dispatch from Duluth, Minnesota, dated Mr. OLIVER.
January 21, which appears in the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' of January 22, 1912. It reads as follows:
The expected advantages to Duluth millers from the granting of a special low rate on grain from the Canadian Northwest to this city, have been dispelled by advices received here that a ruling had been made prohibiting the admitting of this grain unless the duty on it, plus the difference between the regular rate and the special rate, shall first be paid. The ruling is said to be the result of a protest by Canadian millers, who claimed that permission to mill grain here without additional costs could constitute discrimination against them.
I have a further light on that subject contained in an interview which appeared in the Montreal 1 Gazette " of July 11 with Mr. F. W. Thompson, vice-president and managing director of the Ogilvie Flour Mills Company in which he said:
Even Canadian millers may experience considerable difficulty in getting sufficient high grade wheat to fully meet their requirements, and the question of an export duty on the high grade wheats, as a mutter of protection to the home requirements and seed, may with every justification be seriously considered.
I find in the speech that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) delivered in this House on November 23, 1911, the following remarks:
Why should Canada not do the milling business that will go to the millers of Minneapolis?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid that the hon. gentleman is transgressing the" rule. It is not permissible to refer to a previous debate.

I shall not make any further reference to it and I shall not quote any further from it. The rule was not in my mind or I would not have transgressed, I assure you, Mr. Speaker. Action should have been taken by the government according to the knowledge that was in their possession at the time.
The policy of the government, as they are pleased to say, looks to building up the industries and interests of this country of ours by a process of restriction. It. is distinctly in giving effect to that policy that these millions of bushels of damaged wheat in the Northwest are in danger of absolute destruction and it is in pursuance of that policy that the people of the Northwest, the farmers and business men, have lost the millions of dollars that they have lost during the past season from the blockade conditions. There is no escape from the condition. The remedy my hon. friend proposes shall be taken on the 7th of March when, if the newspapers inform us correctly, the rates on barley and flax to Minneapolis and Duluth will be

reduced to the Fort William rates and the rates on wheat and oats will be the rates for grinding in bond and for home consumption as well as for export. But I say that if these conditions had been allowed to prevail at the beginning of the grain blockade on November 10 there would not have been that loss and damage to ^his country that have occurred. If my hon. friends see fit in pursuance of their policy of building up this country by a process of restriction to violate that policy, then it is only right that the country should be made aware of the consequences that are being suffered now by reason 'of that policy. It is too late, I am sorry to say, to save the situation now. My hon. friend has allowed it to go too far, but he shows that he has knowledge of how it could have been saved and he shows that even this process of restriction which he advocates so capably, and which is none the better for his capable advocacy, has broken down and he is compelled by the force of circumstances to abandon it, but he is abandoning it too late. The condition which has existed this past season and which, in the estimation of my hon. friend himself and his colleagues, has called for the abrogation of that- policy of restriction at the last moment when it is too late, may be repeated in future seasons. Probably it will be measurably repeated in all near future seasons unless the country has suffered such a set-back by reason of the results of last season's operations that its expansion in production will be checked.
If, that expansion in production proceeds as rapidly in the future as it has in the past then it will be, if not as neees-say, yet still necessary to find an outlet for our western grains by the shortest rail-haul in future seasons or the country will suffer damage-incalculable damage -such as it has suffered this season. My hon. friend and his colleagues are face to face now with a condition, not a theory. I hope I have been able to impress, that point on their minds and that if they are instrumental in bringing into effect on the 7th March a reduction in grain rates from western points in Minneapolis and Duluth and placing them on the same level as to Fort William they will use the same endeavours to have these rates permanently continued for the benefit of the western producer and for the benefit of the developement of this whole country. I want to ask my hon. friend and those of his colleagues and supporters who believe in that policy of restriction in this country where the benefit to any interest comes out of the loss that is being suffered on the prairies to-day. I ask, is it the banker, is it the merchant, is it the manufacturer, is it the railway company-which of all these interests if benefiting by that
loss? It is a loss to the farmer, it is true, but it is a loss to every other interest in this country. Right in the cities of Toronto and Montreal, the very chapel, the very church, the very cathedral of the doctrine of the restrictive policy, in these ivery centres, the effect of the losses that are being suffered to-day by 'reason of the restrictive policy of the government that is in power, is being felt. Those losses are being suffered in those cities as well as on the prairies of the west. Although we have great confidence in the future of our country, although our country has made great progress in the past and we believe will make good progress in the future I want to warn my hon. friend that it cannot stand a continuation of such shocks and losses as it has suffered this season at the hands of himself and his colleagues and still prosper and progress as we wish it to do.
I would like to know what effect the resolution of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) would have upon the trusts the mergers and the combines; I ,do not think he made that point clear.
If my hon. friend will explain to the House what relation his question bears to the subject I have been dealing with, I will try to answer him.
I thought that was a point the hon. gentleman left out.

STEVENS (Vancouver.) It is not my intention to detain the House at any length in speaking on this question. I certainly congratulate the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) for the exhaustive study he has made of this question, and I also wish to state that a great deal of the information he has gathered will no doubt be of great value to the members of the House and to the public. But, I do not agree entirely with him in the conclusions he has arrived at. In the first place, I think every member of the House will agree that it is a most regrettable thing that this grain blocade prevails to-day in the Northwest Territories. We are all exceedingly sorry that certain losses will occur, but I think it reasonable and fair that we should take info consideration all of the factors that have operated in the causing of this, what we may call, almost a national calamity. The hon. member (Mr. Oliver) has pointed out that there will be considerable monetary loss occurring as the result of the damage to the crops of the Northwest, but the chief object of his speech was to lav upon the shoulders /of the present administration certain responsibility for the prevailing conditions.
That is his whole object.

I wish to draw the attention of the House to some of the causes which have led to the existing conditions. The chief reasons for the conditions which obtain in the northwest at the, present time are natural causes over which no human power has any control. In the first place as pointed out by the hon. member in the quotation he gave from the official bulletin of the Department of Agriculture, the season was a most extraordinary one, wet weather having come in the middle of the year. I think if the hon. gentleman had been as careful to quote the press reports up to about the first of August he would find the utmost optimism running through them, and the cry ' bumper crop * was on the lips of every one from ocean to ocean. We all rejoiced at the prospect of the large crop that the farmers of the west were going to have, but a little later in the season a most unusual thing occurred, when wet and cold weather set in, with the result that the grain did not ripen. That was a condition over which no government had control and against which it was impossible for any human agency to guard. It was consequently, late in the fall before harvesting was begun, and then when harvesting was actually in progress, the continued wet weather hampered further harvesting operations, and threshing. As a matter of fact, a great deal of the grain had been cut green, taking the chance of it drying in the stooks. No matter what your transportation facilities might have been, that grain which was cut partially green, would have been of a much inferior grade, and in all probability would have gone to the elevators in a semi-ripened condition. All these factors are entirely beyond the control of any government or of any human being. Another point I wish to draw attention to, is that, the congestion of grain in the northwest is a thing that will obtain every year, just so long as the farmers of the northwest follow the system of harvesting and marketing which they follow at the present time. A few weeks ago those of us who were not prairie farmers, were told we should mind our own business, and not make suggestions to the farmers of the Northwest, regarding granaries. But, I make bold to state that if the farmers of the Northwest were to provide suitable granaries for their grain, they would experience a great deal less trouble. I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite, who scoff at that idea now, that the time is coming when the farmers of the northwest will have to provide granaries for their grain, and they might just _ as well admit the fact now as later. How in the name of common sense can they expect that the huge harvest in the west in a good season, can be marketed within four or five weeks, and that is really what they are demanding.

They cut their grain, thresh it right out of the stooks, and haul it immediately -to the-market, and expect to have cars enough to carry that grain to the seaboard within a few weeks. It would be far better for the farmers of the west, if they had granaries in which to store their grain, so that they could market it gradually.

Does the hon. gentle, man recall the fact that 150,000 of these farmers are still homesteaders who have gone in within the last four years. How could they be expected to have granaries, considering their financial circumstances?

What the hon. member
says

Mr. CLARK (Red Deer;. They are glad to get shacks.
The hon. member from Red Deer is heard from.
I know all about it.

As a matter of fact it is not the homesteader who has just gone on his land and cropped twenty-five or thirty acres that is to blame; it is the men with four hundred acres, one thousand acres, and two thousand acres who cause the congestion.
They are not the men who suffer.

The man who suffers is the homesteader w'ho has just cropped his few acres of land. I say that it is the system that is followed by the old timers comparatively speaking of the Northwest that is responsible to a large extent for the suffering of the other settlers.

I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens), is familiar with the conditions in the west, and I want to ask him: if a farmer has a granary, the best that ever was built, and his grain is damp when he threshes it or has snow in it, and he stores it in that granary, and it remains until the warm weather sets in, what happens to that grain?

As a matter of fact the condition of the grain when it is threshed is a thing over which no transportation companies or no government can exercise any control whatever, and while it is a matter for regret that that man shall suffer because of that fact, we cannot blame the government, because his grain is wet when he threshes it.
Will the hon. gentleman answer my question?

Yes; I will go a little further; I do not say that a man should1 put his grain in his granary and keep it

there -until the hot weather comes-. The hon. member (Mr. Oliver), is authority for the statement that if it is not moved by May, I think that is w-hat he said.
I said if it is not in the drier by the 1st of April in an ordinarily early spring it is practically gone.

Take it at the first of April, and, therefore, the farmer is not called upon to store his grain until late in the summer. The point is this, that if the farmers had these granaries the bulk of this partially damaged grain, or grain that would be damaged if it is kept into the spring, could be moved1 during the winter months. The hon. member will agree with me that in the majority of seasons the farmer is better off to hold his good grain until May or June.
No.	.

Well, I think that is the case. I will tell you what a number of farmers in the northwest are doing at present, because some of them have told me this themselves.
They get the grain to the market as rapidly as they can, and then play the wheat market in Winnipeg for a rise in the price, and get a profit in that way. They sell their grain in the fall instead of holding it, and then buy wheat on margin in Winnipeg for a rising price. Any number of them do that, and it is a practice for which I have very little sympathy. On the -other hand, if the farmer had his granary, so that he could hold his wheat and sell it whenever he liked, he could control the market and get a better price. But none of the farmers have granaries, and the result is that they are compelled to sell their grain at the price which the owners of the small elevators in the small centres choose to give them. If these elevators are full, the farmer has to keep his grain, and his only choice is to leave it in the fields or bring it to market and sell it at a figure which is arbitrarily fixed by a congested maiket.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know that tin cash price of wheat to-day in Minneapolis is four cents over the May price?
That may be. I am not disputing that fact at all.
Why would the farmer hold his wheat m that case?

It is optional. If a man has his wheat in his granary, he can sell it, or he can hold it and control the market. The reason the market is not steady is that at certain periods of the year it is flooded with grain while at other periods there is not sufficient supply. In any case, if the present system were changed
so that the farmer had granaries in which his grain would be stored, the present conditions would be corn'pletely changed. I quite admit that this year is an extraordinary one. There is a large amount of grain which it is necessary to rush to the drying elevators; but that is accentuated by natural conditions -over which no government could have any control. The hon. member for Edmonton tried to estimate the loss which was sustained in the northwest, saying that 50,000,000 bushels of grain were in the hands of the farmers, of which he admitted that only 30,000,000 bushels were partially damaged. It is well known that a large number of farmers are in the habit of holding their wheat until May, June or July -of the following year, and sometimes it is held over for two years, but not very frequently.
They must have granaries if they do that.

There are a few. The 50,000,000 mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton represent about the average that is held, compared with the full crop this year. So that it is reasonable to say that his estimate of the loss is an exaggeration by at least two or three million dollars. There is no necessity under present conditions of exaggerating the loss that will occur this year, nor is it necessary to draw these pessimistic pictures which have been drawn here for the last couple of months of conditions in the northwest, with one sole object, namely, to cast reflections on the present administration. As a matter of fact, the present administration have done everything that is within human power to do to meet the conditions that obtain in the Northwest at the present time.

Would it not help the farmers in the northwest to have access to the drying facilities in Minneapolis and Duluth, not to mention better prices, and cculd not the government have got that if they had wished?

As a matter of fact, the government have got it. I am perfectly sure that had the hon. member from Edmonton been on the treasury benches at the present time, he could not have done anything more to secure that relief than the present Minister of Trade and Commerce has done.
Reciprocity.

Reciprocity is dead. All that the hon. members of the opposition hoped to have received from reciprocity was access to the American market. If the American people wish to remove the duty from wheat, they can do so, we are not hindering them. All that we refused to do was to pay them a bonus

to remove that duty. When the hon. members trot out reciprocity as a relief to the farmers of the northwest in the the present condition, it is an absolute bugaboo.

The hon. member has not answered my question. I ask: suppose reciprocity had been taken advantage of, and access to the American market had been secured for our farmers, does the hon. member not think that it would have afforded a very substantial measure of relief for them this season?

I do not, for this reason. Had reciprocity passed, it would gimply have made a slight difference_ in the duty on wheat going into the United States.
. Mr. MARTIN (Regina). 25 cents a bushel.

If the American people want our wheat so badly as the hon. members intimate they do, they can remove the duty and get it; but they are not inclined to do that. As a matter of fact, the hon. gentleman's question was fully answered on the 21st of September. The hon. member for Edmonton asks why action was not taken sooner in order to give certain relief which as he suggested could have been given by the Minister. In the same sentence almost he made the statement that the wheat was in the stook, and that it was impossible to harvest and thresh it up to a very recent period. As a matter of fact, throughout the whole northwest to-day every threshing machine, as far as I have been able to learn, is working overtime trying to thresh the grain that has been lying on the ground during the winter. The reason the grain has not been threshed is not because the farmers do not want it threshed, but because there are not the necessary threshing facilities to do it.
My hon. friend has presumed to quote me, and I wish to say that he has not quoted me correctly.

The hon. gentleman will admit that he read a circular as the authority of the government for its knowledge of the conditions, and it set out the exact conditions that I have stated.
During the balance of the season and through certain rains that came on in December, and through a subsequent thaw, and through snow, and so on, it has been impossible to get, thushing done. Now I think I am perfectly correct in that statement, and so I affirm that I care not what the transportation facilities were, the same condition would have obtained, namely, that a large amount of the wheat would have been lying on the ground at the present time in exactly the condition in which it is, because every threshing machine has Mr. STEVENS.
been doing its utmost and working to its full capacity to thresh that grain. Therefore, I want to point out to the hon. members opposite, that the condition which obtains in the northwest to-day in reference to the grain blockade, is to a large extent, or almost entirely, the result of natural conditions, over which no human being has any control, and to the system which obtains in parts of the northwest. Another point is this-I have not the exact figures here, I have not time to secure them, but I think probably the Minister of Trade and Commerce may have them, and will supply them later on-I think some 10,000 cars more were moved within a given time this year by the Canadian Pacific railway than were moved last year or in any other previous year, showing that the transportation companies have done a great deal more to move the grain this year than they ever did before, and that it is unreasonable to expect a transportation company to ha.ve sufficient cars lying idle on the prairies of the Northwest to handle all the wheat, out of the large crop of last year, within the short period of two weeks. Another thing that the transportation companies are faced with is this: A farmer will order a car for, we will say, the 20th of October, or some like date. When that date comes around Mr. Farmer is not prepared to load the car, and he puts his name down the list a month, with the result that while the car may have been assigned to him he is not using it, and it is necessary for the transportation company to switch that car off to some other farmer. This is a matter of common occurrence. I think it is only reasonable and fair that we should take into consideration all the facts of the case, and while I have no brief for any railway or transportation company, not for one moment, at the same time, I do believe that the blockade conditions are due more to natural causes than they are due to the negligence of the railroads in the northwest. I certainly think no case has been made out which would warrant hon. members of this House in condemning the_ administration in this matter, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce should rather be highly commended for his efforts to relieve the situation there, and not only that, but for the introduction of the Grain Bill, which is one of the most up-to-date pieces of legislation which has ever been introduced into this House. I believe that instead of trying to work up an ima-ginery case, based on inferences, and not facts, against the administration, it would be a great deal better if hon. gentlemen opposite had some concrete and reasonable suggestion to make which would assist the administration, rather than to hamper it.

Mr. Speaker, the matter now before the House I consider, as a western mem-

ber and also as a citizen of this Dominion, is one of the most vital questions that has so far been presented for our consideration during the present session, and I believe that every hon. gentleman will agree with me in that view. If western Canada suffers from a car shortage, or suffers in any other respect, so that the people there cannot get returns for their crops, then the rest of Canada must suffer as a result. I have heard gentlemen in this House make the statement that the welfare of eastern Canada depended upon the welfare of western Canada, and I believe most of us will concur in that observation. In considering this matter I want to discuss it as fairly as possible, but before entering upon some arguments in regard to the resolution now before the House. I would like to enlighten the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), although I am afraid any attempt to enlighten that hon. gentleman along the lines indicated in his speech would take up a great deal too much of our time. All that I can say to him is that I would be very glad to exchange my place of abode with him for a few months each year and give him the opportunity to become acquainted close at hand with the conditions in the prairie provinces. I believe that if he had been acquainted with those conditions he would not have made the remarks he did to-night in regard to this question. The hon. gentleman endeavoured to relieve the present government of any blame in connection with the situation in western Canada and he said there were exceptional conditions there, which we all knew of or heard of through the press and from reports that came down from the west. I admit we had to face exceptional conditions, but I urge the government should have immediately proceeded to deal with them in the most drastic manner possible, and should have put into effect what we are urging to-night in this resolution-that is have given the western farmer other trade outlets for his grain, the closest possible outlets, in order to relieve the congestion which has prevailed in the -wept during the past season. That was the duty of the government, and the members on this side are criticising them to-night, because of their inaction in this critical matter. They attempted to afford relief in regard to export grain, but they should have gone further at the same time and given the farmers in the west an opportunity of getting their grain into Minneapolis either for grinding in bond or for consumption in the United States. I can tell hon. gentlemen that there was a ready demand for the grain of western Canada in Minneapolis. I had a statement
riiade to me by a gentleman from western Canada, who was in the elevator business, or at least is in touch with large interests there, that the representatives of one of the grain growers' associations of Saskatchewan went down to Minneapolis and ascertained that they could sell there to a commission house 100 cars each of every grade of grain up to No. 6, and also what is known as Feed Wheat. They could have sold that grain in the markets of Minneapolis. All they wanted was to get a better railroad rate and they could have obtained, even after paying the duty, a better price for their grain than could be got in Canada. I was informed of that condition by a man who is intimately acquainted with the elevator business in the province of Saskatchewan. I want to say that if we had had in western Canada a crop such as seemed probable in the early part of the season, we would have had the greatest crop that the west ever had. If we had had that crop and ideal conditions for harvesting, the railroads there simply could not have handled it any more than they are in a position to handle the crop that we actually had this year smaller and damaged though it was.
I also want to point out to my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) that when he states that the railroads have been keeping in touch with the advance of western Canada in regard to the supplying of cars, he is, in my opinion, entirely mistaken. I do not believe that the railroads have been keeping in touch with the growth of the country in that respect, and I think one of the reasons for the car shortage this year is that the railroads have not the motive power and have not the cars available to relieve the prevailing congestion. In my part of the province of Alberta-and I had occasion to draw the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the conditions there some time ago-they have now" the first car shortage they ever experienced. I believe that particular part of western Canada is in better shape this year than any other part of the country, I believe that more of its crop is threshed and ready to be shipped than in any other district of the various provinces. Nevertheless they have a car shortage. I would like to point this out: I know a farmer in the vicinity of a village called Barons, near the city of Lethbridge, who was 294th on the list for a car at that station. He was 294th on the list in the early part of September of last year and up to the first of this month he had not been able to get a car. That is in the southern part of the province of Alberta. I also have the statement that a farmer in the vicinity of High River had only been able to get one car since December 31st. He wrote me to that effect in the beginning of this month, and he said there

400S
were 144 cars at that time on the order book at the station of High River. Now these are simply two instances to show that the Canadian Pacific railway in that particular part of the country has not been able to keep up with the demand for cars. They have not been sufficiently acquainted with the crop conditions and the need of cars to supply the demand in that particular section of the west. The railways are not prepared to meet the emergency, and I say more that the railways are responsible, to a considerable extent, for the prevailing conditions. Now let me explain that statement. The railways in the west make the announcement very freely that they are going to build a certain branch line immediately. Two instances of that occurred in my own district. For instance the Canadian Northern company announced two or three years ago that it was going to rush the Goose Lake branch of its line. People flocked in there and homesteaded in that country. Others bought what land they could buy, they have been in there for two or three years, they have had to raise crops in order to live, and some of them have had to go 70 to 80 miles to sell and to ship their grain. These' people would not have gone into that district if the railroad had not induced them to go in there by stating it was going to build that branch line immediately. A similar instance has occurred in the southern part of Alberta, in that part of the country south of the Crows Nest branch of the Canadian Pacific railway which is thickly settled.
The people have to go from fifty to sixty miles to sell their grain. These people went into the country because the Canadian ' Pacific railway promised to build the Wey-burn branch, and they thought that that line was to be immediately put under construction. And now we find that construction is only to commence this year. The railways have encouraged the people to come into the country; they encouraged them to raise crops. Yet, when they do raise crops, they have to go fifty or sixty miles to a station, and when they get there they find that the Canadian Pacific railway cannot supply them with cars and that there is no elevator accommodation. Frequently these farmers have to go back with their grain that distance. It means practically a complete loss of the crop. My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has had something to say about storage. He advises the farmers of western Canada to store their grain, and wait until they have a favourable opportunity , to sell it. The hon. gentleman is totally out of touch with the conditions in western Canada. Those farmers who are in the best financial position provide storage facilities. But he must understand that the people who are going on homesteads in our west, Mr. BUCHANAN.
are people, as a rule, with very little capital. They come to the west to make a home and a fortune for themselves. Most of them have been there but a few years, and the greater part of their money has been spent in building a home and barns, and in purchasing machinery at the high protection prices they have to pay. They must sell their crop as soon as they possibly can, in order to get the money to meet their payments. They cannot afford to store their grain and hold it until the Canadian Pacific railway or some other railway can supply them with cars or the elevator can afford them storage. They do not want to store their wheat, and cannot store it under present circumstances. Something was said by my hon. friend from Vancouver also with respect to reciprocity. He expressed the views that I expected he would, when he said that reciprocity was practically a bonus to the United States. Those of us who lived in western Canada, do not so regard it. We think that recipro-procity would have met a situation such as that which has arisen. But we believe that the attitude the people of Canada took on that occasion was a bonus to eastern Canada, and not to the advantage of western Canada. And I believe that the manufacturers and interests of eastern Canada, in taking the action they did on September 21, did the thing which was most injurious to themselves. I found this feeling among our western farmers during the discussion of reciprocity. Reciprocity would be helpful to^ them and would not injure any of the interests of eastern Canada; but, in the face of that, the men who have been made rich by the development that has taken place and the business they have secured from the farmers of the west have opposed what was considered by the farmers of the west to be in their own interest. If there is any cleavage between east and west, it is not due to what the farmers, did on the 21st of September, but- to what Ihe manufacturers of eastern Canada did on that day. I believe we have in eastern Canada people who will soon come to realize that it is in the interest of all Canada that the farmers should have the opportunity to sell their grain in the nearer market of the United States. What we want is the larger market and nearer market, and I believe that the people of the east will come to'realize the benefit that that will afford to the whole country, as we have realized it already. We are simply demanding in this resolution that we should be given an opportunity to sell our grain in the United States markets, with a railroad rate which is better than that afforded us at the present time. We believe that the government had an opportunity to relieve the situation I that has arisen from this blockade which

commenced six months ago and it sadly neglected to provide it.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. E. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rather long and exhaustive speech of my hon. friend of Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) had a good deal in it which was an attack upon Providence, but it ended up with an attack directed against the government and particularly against the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the ground that he had not performed the duty he might have performed. The one question that came to me over and over again while my hon. friend was speaking might be expressed in the old Latin words ' Cui Bono?' I could not but ask myself as he was speaking, what is the good of all this that he is saying? A man in the responsible position of my hon. friend, an old and tried statesman, one who has been a member of the government for years, is not generally supposed to occupy the time of a deliberative assembly unless he has something in view for the benefit of the public. The first half of his speech, taking up an hour or more, was devoted to detailing the hard usage which nature and Providence had dealt out to the western farmer during the last season. What remedy does my hon. friend propose? He cannot move a vote of want of confidence in nature and Providence. If he did it would not have much effect; he would not be able to turn nature and Providence out of office or change their action. He detailed with minute particularity the loss to the farmer in the west.
The first thing they lost was a slice of their expectations. For some reason or other they ploughed, they harrowed and sowed their seed, and came to the conclusion that if Providence was at all fair to them they ought to get 225 million bushels. It turned out they only got about 175 million bushels; there was a big slice off their expectations. Does my hon. friend blame the government for that? Worse-still happened. Not sufficiently satisfied with cutting a slice off their expectations -not asking here whether their expectations were pitched1 too high or not-not satisfied with that, Providence continued to pour too much rain down, and give inlet to too little of the sun's rays. So the crop, instead of ripening as it should have, continued to grow rather than to ripen, refused to ripen, and the season was, we will say, a month late. Is my hon. friend going to move a vote of want of confidence in the government because the sun refused to shine with sufficient brilliancy, because the heavens refused to be economical of their stores, and were lavish during all that month? It is a thing for which nobody is to blame or can be blamed, and a thing which could not
have been avoided, even if somebody had acted as somebody should have acted.
There was another point to be taken. Contrary to the wishes of the government, there occurred a row between the miners and the mine owners, and the miners refused to work without certain conditions, and the mine owners refused to come up to those conditions. Work stopped in the mines, and a thing which, in some respects, is just as bad as the loss of the harvest, threatened the people of the northwest. The very farmers and dwellers that my hon. friend is rightly concerned about, were threatened with a coal famine. My hon. friend knows that. Does he blame the government for that? The railways had to meet the situation; and, talk as you will about the railways, and rail against them as some people who are not over thoughtful, do, talk as you will and rave against them, the railways came to the aid1 of that situation in the northwest, and they took 600,000 tons and mere of coal and spread it througn all portions of the northwest, in order to provide against a possible famine and a possible freezing in consequence of a coal famine. That took a great deal of the available resources of the transport companies. They carried their cars, subject to delay, and with these heavy burdens of traffic, carried them to all parts of the northwest. When these were unloaded and were ready for transport -out, the season was so far behind and the harvest was so unready for shipment, that there was not grain to be put into these cars to be taken back at that particular time. Does my hon. friend propose to move a vote of want of confidence in the government because of that occurrence and the consequent disruption of business?
In what direction was the coal hauled by these cars?
It was not hauled easterly. So I will allow my hon. friend to exercise his judgment to find in what direction it was hauled.
The coal was hauled westerly. In which direction was the grain hauled?
The largest part of the grain was hauled easterly.
My hon. friend will have to be more than amusing in order to satisfy the House that hauling coal westward prevented the hauling of grain eastward at the samp. time.
My hon. friend has made his rejoinder to that after I had stated the facts of the case. If the grain was not ready to be hauled it could not be placed in the cars for hauling.
Then the hauling of coal west did not have any effect on the case.

My hon. friend does not know much about the transport conditions, if he does not know of that shortage of coal in the west, and if he does not know that the hauling of that coal resulted in disorganization and confusion to the railway traffic. He will only have to talk to railroad managers to understand that, but I think he does understand it. There was then another thing that operated very hardly. The harvest was late in coining to maturity and afterwards was late in coming to the point where it could be transported. The season was, as my hon. friend admitted, at least a month or a month and a half shorter for haulage purposes. Thus you had a larger output of grain to be hauled, and you had the hauling season a month or a month and a half later than it usually began, and consequently the railway was deprived of that 'much of the time for the transport of the grain. Now take all these things into consideration, and going no further than the time of the freezing of the lakes and the stoppage of lake traffic, the disadvantage that the railroads were under from these reasons was a great disavantage.. But, there is something more than that, and let us state it to be perfectly fair. Blame the railway as much as you reasonably can but do put the other side at least when you are making up the whole account and let us see what lies to the credit of the transportation companies as well as the disadvantages under which they labour.
My hon. friend went on to say that not only were there late crops and a diminution in the expected1 crops, but that there was also a degradation in quality, and he makes an elaborate calculation as to how much the farmers of the northwest have lost by a depreciation of price owing to the poorer quality of the grain. My hon. friend went on to draw this gloomy picture. What boots it to have drawn such a gloomy picture as this? It seems to be almost like a man who had suffered from wounds by accidents and who was laid up in the hospital; he gets out of it, gets back to his home, and is able to move fairly comfortably. Some kind friend knocks at the front door and when he goes to the front door the friend hauls him out, tears apart every one of his wounds, takes every plaster off the healing bruises, drags him out into the light of day, and shows him to his neighbours with his wounds uncovered and freshly opened, but he applies to them no balm, he pours no oil into them. What kind of a mind must a man have - who expects to help his neighbour by that kind of treatment? So I thought and when my hon. friend was speaking I asked again the question: What good is coming out of all this? What man is to be helped by opening his wounds afresh? Does it give him
greater hope, instil into him a greater spirit of optimism, put into him courage and vigour? I do not think it does. Does it help Canada as a whole to have that dull, dark picture brought again to view, not once, or twice but for the tenth or eleventh time? Surely we want as bright an atmosphere and as hopeful an outlook as possible. What in the world would become of us as a community if when a man got sick all sorts of physical troubles were portrayed to him. So my hon. friend was not doing any good to the farmer of the northwest and he was not doing any good to the reputation of Canada. But, he says, this present government do not seem to have alleviated the situation. What about himself and his own government? Had not he the Northwest Territories in his hand?
