Then, of course, when my hon. friend was in the vein of bad logic he could not get off the use of the tu quoque. He says that my hon. friend has slept with the west. Wonderful discovery. He says, you have walked with the west. A very original idea. But he says, what did you do to relieve the evils? We provided a remedy, which you misled the country to turn down. Then my hon. friend goes on to say, what reformatory steps ought to be taken? And he gets back to his old calling of an instructor of the farmers. He says, you have got to improve your methods of cultivation. If we improve our methods of cultivation what will be one of the first results? Increased crops, more grain to dispose of. So my hon. friend's method of treating a grain blockade is to double the amount of grain he has got to handle. He has got more to handle now than he can take care of, and his recom-
.FEBRUARY 28, 1912
ruendation to the western farmers is, improve your methods of cultivation, double your crop, and then you will get rid of your grain. Then of course mixed farming came in. Well, now the difficulty with my hon. friend, as with some others who have spoken here is that they really do not know the west. There are places in Saskatchewan where you cannot water your stock within seven miles of your farm buildings. In addition to that, when men go into the west they go for the purpose of tilling large quantities of land, and taking advantage of that very wheat production which my hon. friend is condemning here, which is the secret of Canada's prosperity to-day, the secret of the growth of the cities of which you are so proud. Then my hon. friend went on to give other directions to the farmers. He says they have got to store their grain. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) gave the same advice. Well, now I speak with some knowledge on this question, and I want to tell my hon. friends in all good faith that I have been living ten years among those people, I have been endeavouring to make my livelihood upon the western lands, and I want to assure them that when men go into that western country they have to make a careful reckoning of cents and dollars before they undertake any expenditure whatever. I do not know the owner of a homestead who would not be anxious to improve his buildings, improve his dwelling house, I do not know one in my own neighbourhood. But I know that a large number of them have a great anxiety to keep out of debt. They want to get along in the world. I intend to preach this doctrine to eastern Canadians, _ because a large number of eastern Canadians are only removed two generations from the time when their own forefathers were going through the same trials and difficulties that the western pioneers are going through to-day. To tell a man who has got to his last dollar that he must build barns is rather an unfeeling way to approach this problem. I make that personal appeal with an intimate knowledge of the conditions. But I want to go a step further. My hon. friend says, store the grain. How far will that carry you? We do not raise grain to store it, but we raise grain to sell it. We raise it to get it to its final repository, which is the stomach of a human being, either in this country or some other country. If you store your grain, and go on and break up your soil and produce more for next year, does my hon. friend not see that lie simply moves his problem six months back, and that the next year things will be worse than they are now? The farmer cannot build a granary in every field. I think that is a fair way of looking at it.
But there is an additional reason under this head, why I think this is an absolutely insufficient and paltry remedy to offer to the farmer. The farmer has to sell his grain in the fall, because, apart from the mere matter of a living, he need's the money to pay his way. What is the use of telling a farmer who is being worried by the representative of a firm of implement dealers in Toronto for a high price for his implements, and who has interest to pay on that price to store his grain? The implement agent does not say that; he says: here is your note, can you settle it? Between the implement dealer who says: here is my note, can you settle it? and my friend who says: store your grain, the farmer is in a pretty tight position. I am the farmer, I feel that difficulty. I hope that my hon. friend, when he talks about barns and storehouses-and he reminds me of the foolish man in the Scripture when he does it-will deal with this point, and that he will tell me how the farmers of western Canada are going to get out of this difficulty.
I do not know that there was a great deal in the speech of the hon. gentleman further than what I have already dealt with, but I am far from having said all I want to say on this problem, because when I rose I promised to endeavour to show to the government that it was a bigger problem than they have any comprehension of. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said: What is the use of fighting the battles of last September again? He re-echoed a remark in tne speech of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and it had been re-echoed already by the hon. member for Vancouver from the maiden speech of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White), in this House. I do not want to fight any battle of this life over again except in so far as I can learn lessons from it for the future battles of this life. I take it that it is the duty of the government, who are responsible for dealing with the affairs of the country, to solve this problem. We are all alike in being anxious to do the best we can for Canada. I would like to say to my hon. friend's that they might happen to have on this reciprocity question a change of heart and a change of mind. I know that none of us can teach the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce anything about the great principles of politics. He knows, if any man knows in this House, that, as Mr. Asquith said the other day, there is no finality in politics. It is excusable in the hon. member for Vancouver, it is excusable in an inexperienced member like the Minister of Finance, to say that reciprocity is dead. That is the kind of political opinion we expect from such inexperienced quarters, but I know that, like Mr. Asquith, the

pire that I would sever, politically speaking, from another particle of dust in the British Empire. I believe that the British Empire is the greatest engine that the world has seen up to now for the propagation in this world of the principles of freedom and justice, and I would not lift my little finger to break or hurt that empire in any way or to sever the sections of the integral portions of that empire. But when we are talked to in that way as to the necessity of maintaining a proper connection between the East and the West I want to say in conclusion that the only way you will maintain it is in the way my hon. friend indicated: by tackling manfully these problems, and if my hon. friends opposite are to be allowed to imagine all they like about building a few railroads I ask them to extend their imagination to the production of some hundreds of millions of more bushels of wheat than Britain can possibly take, and then I ask them where they are going to turn for a market. Consistency has been described as the last infirmity of noble minds-let me concede to my hon. friends all the nobleness of mind they like but I say to them: for goodness sake don't hang on to the last, infirmity.
Look into the history of your own party and see if there is not yet time to turn in the one direction in which you can turn for a ready and larger market for your products. We can only solve the problem' of east and west by the sincere spirit of the closing words of my hon. friend. Now, I want to put this to my hon. friends in the east: if they were western farmers, would their attachment to the east be increased by your saying to them: produce your wheat, it is a beautiful thing to grow wheat, sell it if you can after we have built the Hudson Bay railway and have made a way out for it through the icebergs to a limited market; hut do not sell it to the Yankees; they eat wheat and will pay a good price for it, but they should not eat Canadian wheat; do not sell it to them. If you were a farmer in the west would you he bound by ties of affection to the people of eastern Canada if they said: we are going to put all the obstacles possible in the way of vour selling your produce, and at the same time we are going to take the last cent out of you by preventing you from buying where you like? I do not think anything can shake the loyalty of the west, and I want to say that there is no section of the people of the west who are more loyal than our recent American immigrants. I want to pay that testimony to them. Nine out of ten of them say: we prefer the laws of this country to the laws of the United States, and to that extent they are loyal; but their loyalty will not he strengthened by the Mr. CLARK (Red Deer).
kind of treatment I have described. You cannot show your affection for a man by hanging around his neck with one arm and rifling his pocket with the other. It is not a square deal to tell us, You must be restricted where you sell and equally restricted where you buy. This question will have to be carefully looked into. I really think from the careful way in which my hon. friend is following me that he is taking this thing seriously, and I have good hopes that he will look into this question thoroughly. Let him throw consistency to the winds, as all the great statesmen have done. Sir Robert Peel went into power in 1841 pledged to maintain protection, and in 1846 repealed the com laws; and the people of Huddersfield erected to his memory a monument which I walk around every time I visit that town and read the inscription on it. Let the hon. gentleman throw consistency to the winds and deal squarely with this problem, and then you will see a prosperous Canada, a Canada that will be the marvel of the world because I think that with a proper economic system and good government it is destined to be the greatest nation on earth.

The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has treated the House to a dissertation the major portion of which consisted of platitudes uttered with a loud voice and in a bumptious manner that rejoiced hon. gentlemen on that side of the House who mistook noise for argument. The hon. gentleman, during the course of his somewhat discursive speech, the best portion of which consisted of quotations from John Morley on Gladstone, took occasion to read to this House a lesson on parliamentary ethics. The hon. gentleman seemed to find, fault with a harmless and innocent remark that was made on this side of the House while he was speaking. The words used were, ' go easy,' surely harmless, innocent words, that one would think would not call forth the diatribe that we heard from til? hio. mcmbi i. The hon. member told us aboat the mother of parliaments. It strikes me, judging from the usual condition of tie hon. m.unbor for Red Deer, that he is rn.tih better acquainted with the purlieus of Whitechapel and Seven Dials than he if with West minster.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. Everybody knows that Whitechapel is a district where you will find the lowest class that inhabits the city of London, and I think it is an injurious remark for any hon. gentleman to suggest that another hon. member of this House is fitted to he an inhabitant of those purlieus.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The remark was scarcely within the amenities of the debates of parliament, and I would ask the hon. member (Mr. Fowler) to withdraw it.

Mr Speaker, just a moment

.
Order, chair.
You will permit me to say that many very good people, actuated by the very best motives, go into the purlieus of Whitechapel.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is only making the offence worse attempting to justify the remark. I think it would be more appropriate to withdraw it.

In deference to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, if I have made use of any remark which is unparliamentary, which if it were not for your ruling I would not consider so, I will of course come within the parity rule and withdraw the remark. But at the same time, I have a right to say this, that the personal remarks made by the hon. member for Red Leer were quite as injurious, as far as I was concerned, as anything I said about him. The hon. gentleman has told us that he himself is a farmer; aud, Sir, if any argument were needed to back up the statement made by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce that a considerable part of the difficulty in the country was due to bad farming, the statement made by the hon. member for Red Deer that he is a farmer would amply supply that argument. it is a remarkable thing that men .who have been failures in every other sphere of life, hearing of those fertile lands in the west have gone there hoping to achieve success, and that is one of the ills that this country is suffering from at the present time. I will not say that there are not other ills. I will not say that the transportation facilities are yet sufficient to carry out the products of the country. But it does seem to me that what the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out is absolutely true, that the fault cannot lie with the government, who have not had either time or opportunity to take this matter into proper consideration and provide the necessary remedy.
But, Sir, the fault does lie at the door of hon. gentlemen opposite, and mainly and principally at the door of the exMinister of the Interior, the man who moved this resolution. Because. Sir, charged as he was to look after the interests of the people of the west he took no steps whatever to provide the necessary remedy for evil which he never saw impending but which was rapidly approaching. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) in dealing with this matter can only hark back to the old threadbare subject of reciprocity, a subject which was threshed out in this country from end to end, and which the people of Canada voted against with such almost surprising unanimity on the 21st of September last. The hon gentleman is not original at all. He never makes a speech in this House in which he does, not discuss the question of reciprocity. That seems to be the only tiling on which he can talk with any lucidity at all, that is the very thing which is troubling him most. The hon. gentleman also says:	You cannot expect Britain to
take your grain no matter what means of transportation you may supply, no matter how you may increase the facilities for carrying that grain to the markets of the world. Then what country is going to take it? ' Oh, tile United States '. Mr. Speaker, the lack of knowledge the hon. gentleman has with regard to farming, the lack of knowledge that he has, with regard to parliamentary ethics is to be regretted. The same hon. gentleman quoted my allusion to Whitechapel and was so lacking in proper respect to members of this House as to refer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce as ' My frivolous old friend'. The hon gentleman holds himself at all times as conforming to the proper parliamentary attitude as observed m the Mother of parliaments, where they almost fought across the benches on one occasion a few months ago. We have not yet come to that in this House, although with the example of the hon. member for Red Deer before us I do not know to what length we may ultimately go. Well, Sir, he has told us that the great remedy, the sovereign panacea, the cure-all for the ills from which the people of western Canada are suffering to-day, is to send their grain away to the United States which to-day exports more wheat than we in Canada raise altogether. That is the sort of remedy this great and wonderful statesman from- 1 will not say Whitechapel because you Mr. Speaker, have said that I should not use the term-but this great and wonderful statesman this modern miracle worker in statesmanship is able to supply to the people of western Canada. It seems to me that nothing could be more absurd, robbed as I say of its noise and its quotations from Gladstone, than the speech we have listened to to-night from the hon. member for Red Deer.
